title: Whole Transcriptome Sequencing Reveals a GATA4-INHA Program and Progenitor Cell of Origin in Cholangioblastic Cholangiocarcinoma.
journal: Modern pathology : an official journal of the United States and Canadian Academy of Pathology, Inc
abstract: Cholangioblastic cholangiocarcinoma (CBCA) is a rare hepatobiliary neoplasm defined by the NIPBL::NACC1 fusion. Its cell of origin and nomenclature remain unresolved, and some investigators favor reclassification as a fusion-positive hepatic carcinoma rather than a distinctive cholangiocarcinoma variant. We used whole transcriptome sequencing (WTS) to define the CBCA transcriptional program and differentiation state relative to other hepatobiliary malignancies. In total, 334 hepatobiliary neoplasms were subjected to WTS from multiple institutions, spanning eight diagnostic categories including 10 CBCA and 163 intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA). Clustering, differential expression, gene set enrichment, immune deconvolution, and cell-of-origin analyses were performed, and GATA4 immunohistochemistry was validated on an independent cohort of 445 cases. The NIPBL::NACC1 fusion gene was identified in all 10 CBCA and in none of the remaining 324 neoplasms. Diagnostic category accounted for 52.7% of transcriptomic variance (p=0.001), and CBCA formed a discrete cluster nearest iCCA despite limited gene-level overlap, and harbored more differentially expressed genes than any category (n=1,451 vs. all combined). GATA4 was upregulated (log2FC=3.23, p<0.001), with upregulation of 14 of 33 GATA4 target genes including INHA (largest fold change), corresponding to GATA4 protein overexpression in 6 of 6 CBCA, 2% of iCCA, and 0 of 278 HCC. Synaptic and neuroendocrine programs were the most enriched pathways, and cell-of-origin analysis placed CBCA in an intermediate biliary progenitor state with the highest Bipotency Index of any category (p≤0.001) and near-complete immune exclusion. Together, these findings define a GATA4-INHA transcriptional program downstream of NIPBL::NACC1 that accounts for the inhibin A immunophenotype of CBCA. This biliary progenitor state supports the cholangioblastic designation over a hepatocellular carcinoma origin, confirmed at the protein level by GATA4 immunohistochemistry.

title: SCN2B Drives Depression-like Phenotypes in Mice by Suppressing BDNF Signaling via Its Intracellular Domain NICD.
abstract: The rising global burden of depression necessitates novel mechanistic insights and therapeutic targets. Voltage-gated sodium channel β2-subunit (Navβ2, coded by SCN2B) has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders, yet its role in depression remains unexplored. Here, we identify SCN2B as a previously unrecognized driver of depression-like pathophysiology. Using SCN2B-overexpressing (SCN2B-OV) mice across different ages (1, 12, and 20 months) and CRISPR- engineered Navβ2V173A,V175K mice with selective reduction of the Navβ2 intracellular domain (NICD), we combined behavioral phenotyping, electrophysiology, neurotransmitter profiling, and molecular analyses, with chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) as an environmental challenge. SCN2B-OV mice exhibited accelerated depression-like phenotypes, including anhedonia (sucrose preference 52.42% reduction, P<0.05), behavioral despair (forced swim test immobility 67.42% increase, P<0.05), and cognitive deficits (Y-maze alternation 50.90% reduction, P<0.05), independent of natural aging. Electrophysiologically, SCN2B overexpression induced a striking prefrontal-hippocampal imbalance: prefrontal cortex (PFC) became hyperexcitable (glutamate release increased by 64.7%; sEPSC amplitude increased 2.05-fold, P<0.05), whereas the hippocampus showed synaptic suppression (GABA release reduced by 32.65%; sIPSC frequency reduced by 66.67%, P<0.05). Mechanistically, SCN2B overexpression suppressed BDNF/TrkB/PI3K/AKT signaling axis (BDNF reduced by 53.17%; p-TrkB reduced by 63.62%, P<0.05), accompanied by decreased synaptic proteins (PSD95 43.45%, synapsin I 40.31%, P<0.05). Remarkably, NICD-reduced Navβ2V173A,V175K mice were fully resistant to CUMS-induced behavioral and neurotransmitter deficits, establishing NICD as a critical mediator of stress vulnerability. Collectively, these findings unravel a causal pathway in which SCN2B overexpression drives NICD-dependent suppression of BDNF signaling, leading to region-specific excitatory/inhibitory imbalance, synaptic disintegration, and depression-like phenotypes. Targeting Navβ2 proteolysis to block NICD generation may thus represent a novel therapeutic strategy for mood disorders.

title: Insights into CD36/P-gp involvement in dietary lipid-driven PAH transport across the blood-brain barrier.
abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), as widespread environmental contaminants, exhibit neurotoxicity. Because PAHs often co-occur with dietary lipids in foods, those lipids might serve as vehicles that alter PAH biotransport and accumulation in the brain. In this work, we systematically investigated how three common dietary fatty acids-oleic acid, linoleic acid (LA), and linolenic acid-differently influence the transport steps (including cellular uptake, efflux, and clearance) of benzo[a]pyrene (BaP) and benzo[b]fluoranthene (BbF) across the blood-brain barrier, using a bEnd.3 cell-based model, and explored the potential underlying molecular mechanisms. Results revealed that dietary lipids, acting as carriers, significantly enhanced cellular uptake of PAHs, with LA increasing the uptake of BaP and BbF by 20.36% and 17.90%, respectively, and accelerated transmembrane transport dynamics. Simultaneously, distinct lipids differentially affected PAH clearance and efflux. Notably, LA delayed the clearance of PAHs, prolonging the elimination half-life of BaP from 10.117 h to 17.696 h and that of BbF from 7.418 h to 14.964 h, thereby increasing overall brain exposure. Mechanistically, LA was observed to upregulate the fatty acid transporter CD36, and functional inhibition studies suggested that P-glycoprotein and CD36 may jointly contribute to lipid-modulated effects. This study suggests that dietary lipids influence brain exposure to PAHs through a multi-level network, highlighting a factor that warrants consideration when assessing their neurotoxicity risks.

title: A multimodal MRI study of DTI-ALPS and cerebral blood flow changes across the Alzheimer's disease continuum.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by cerebral blood flow (CBF) abnormalities and alterations in the neurofluid-related brain tissue environment, but their evolution along the AD continuum and links to cognitive decline and plasma biomarkers remain unclear. Using multimodal MRI, we quantified the diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index and CBF alterations and examined their associations with cognitive performance and plasma biomarkers across the AD continuum. This study enrolled 78 healthy controls (HC), 53 subjective cognitive decline (SCD), 40 mild cognitive impairment (MCI), 110 AD. All subjects received MRI and neurocognitive assessments. The DTI-ALPS index was used as a diffusion-based marker of directional water diffusivity within periventricular white matter and the neurofluid-related tissue environment. CBF changes were calculated, and plasma biomarkers associated with neurodegeneration were measured. Partial correlation analysis explored relationships among ALPS index, CBF in cognition-related brain regions, cognitive scores, and plasma biomarkers. Statistical mediation analyses were performed to assess indirect effects involving the ALPS index and plasma biomarkers in the association between regional CBF and cognitive performance. ALPS index decreased stage-dependently along the AD continuum, significantly lower in MCI and AD versus HC and SCD. HC and SCD showed higher CBF than AD in right middle cingulate and left inferior parietal lobule. CBF in bilateral angular gyri and right superior frontal gyrus positively correlated with MoCA and RAVLT scores. Cognition-related CBF positively correlated with bilateral mean ALPS index, and negatively with NfL and p-tau217. Statistical mediation analyses identified significant indirect effects involving the bilateral mean ALPS index and plasma NfL in the association between regional CBF and cognitive performance. Cerebral hypoperfusion, altered DTI-ALPS measures, and axonal injury were closely associated across the AD continuum, suggesting interrelated neurovascular, neurofluid-related tissue, and neurodegenerative alterations associated with cognitive impairment.

title: Elimination profile of dexamethasone in dried blood spots (DBS) following single and multiple oral administration and proposal of the minimum reporting level to distinguish forbidden from allowed administrations in sports drug testing.
journal: European journal of pharmaceutical sciences : official journal of the European Federation for Pharmaceutical Sciences
abstract: Glucocorticoids (GC), such as dexamethasone (DEX), are prohibited in sports competitions when administered by systemic routes including oral, injectable, and rectal administrations. Since they remain permitted by other therapeutic routes, Minimum Reporting Levels (MRLs) are required to detect misuse in sports. Although antidoping analyses are mainly performed in urine, increasing interest has recently focused on alternative matrices such as dried blood spots (DBS). In this study, the suitability of DBS for the detection of DEX and the evaluation of its elimination profile was investigated. A liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry method was developed for the quantification of DEX and its main metabolite, 6β-hydroxy-DEX, in DBS. The method showed good linearity, sensitivity, precision, and accuracy, with no significant matrix effects. It was applied to samples collected after oral administration of DEX in healthy male participants following single-dose (4 mg, n=8) and multiple-dose (2 × 2 mg/day for 5 days, n=8) regimens. DEX and its metabolite reached the highest concentrations within the first 4 h post-administration and were generally detectable up to 24 h, without evidence of accumulation after repeated dosing. Cortisol suppression was observed in all participants, confirming the systemic effect of oral DEX administration. Plasma samples collected at the same time points showed similar concentration profiles, suggesting homogeneous distribution of DEX between plasma and red blood cells. Based on the DBS-to-plasma ratio obtained and literature plasma data, an MRL of 2 ng/mL in DBS was proposed to identify prohibited systemic DEX administration during sports competitions.

title: Alginate Oligosaccharide Alleviates Age-Related Hearing Loss via TFEB-Associated Autophagy Restoration to Attenuate Oxidative Stress and Inflammation.
journal: European journal of pharmaceutical sciences : official journal of the European Federation for Pharmaceutical Sciences
abstract: Age-related hearing loss (ARHL) is a highly prevalent sensory disorder characterized by progressive cochlear degeneration. To date, no effective pharmacological treatment is clinically available. In this study, we investigated the otoprotective efficacy and underlying mechanisms of alginate oligosaccharide (AOS) against D-galactose (D-gal)-induced senescence in vitro and age-associated cochlear dysfunction in C57BL/6J mice. Multi-omics analyses identified oxidative stress, inflammation, cellular senescence, and autophagy, as core targeted pathways associated with AOS treatment. In D-gal-treated HEI-OC1 cells and cochlear explants, AOS treatment markedly reduced senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity and downregulated senescence markers P16 and P21. These anti-senescent effects were accompanied by ameliorated oxidative and pro-inflammatory stress, as reflected by decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS), preserved mitochondrial function, and suppressed nuclear factor-κB/NOD-like receptor pyrin domain-containing 3 (NF-κB/NLRP3) signaling. AOS also promoted transcription factor EB (TFEB) nuclear translocation and attenuated D-gal-induced autophagy-related dysregulation. Pharmacological inhibition of autophagy and TFEB nuclear entry effectively blunted these cytoprotective, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory benefits of AOS, supporting the involvement of TFEB-associated autophagic signaling in AOS-mediated protection. In C57BL/6J mice, long-term AOS administration significantly lowered auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds, attenuated the age-related degeneration of hair cells and spiral ganglion neurons, and reduced cochlear senescence markers. Furthermore, AOS suppressed MDA accumulation, elevated SOD activity, inhibited NF-κB/NLRP3 activation, and restored TFEB-associated autophagic homeostasis in vivo. Collectively, these findings suggest that AOS protects against age-associated cochlear dysfunction and senescence, accompanied by reduced oxidative stress and inflammation and improved autophagy-related homeostasis. TFEB-associated signaling may contribute to these protective effects, supporting further investigation of AOS for the prevention or delay of cochlear aging.

title: Regular exercise augments gut-brain communication and visceral feedback control of appetite.
abstract: Regular exercise is widely accepted to support long-term body weight management; however, the neurobiological adaptations that contribute to the beneficial effects of habitual physical activity beyond increases in energy expenditure per se remain unclear. Here, we investigated whether regular exercise alters gut-brain communication and visceral feedback control of feeding. Mice were subjected to regular voluntary wheel running. Energy expenditure and feeding were assessed under basal conditions and following an overnight fast. Nutrients were delivered directly into the stomach by intragastric infusion. Brain-wide responses to intragastric nutrient delivery were assessed using positron emission tomography (PET). Single-cell sequencing and histological analyses were used to determine nutrient-responsive neuronal populations in the caudal brainstem. Genetic associations with body weight were evaluated using GWAS data. Intragastric nutrient delivery suppressed feeding more strongly in exercising mice. Brain-wide PET revealed enhanced responses to intragastric nutrients in various brain regions. Single-cell sequencing identified several nutrient-responsive caudal brainstem populations, including a previously unrecognized population marked by expression of fibrinogen C domain containing 1 (FIBCD1). Regular exercise selectively enhanced the nutrient-evoked activation of FIBCD1 neurons. Histological analyses demonstrate that FIBCD1 neurons are also present in the human brainstem, and GWAS data suggest a potential relevance of this neuron population to body-weight regulation. Regular exercise enhances behavioral and brain responses to intragastric nutrient delivery and sensitizes FIBCD1 neurons in the brainstem of mice. These findings reveal an exercise-associated adaptation of gut-brain communication that may contribute to improved matching of caloric intake to energy expenditure.

title: Simultaneous brain-spinal fMRI reveals neural mechanisms of TENS-induced analgesia.
abstract: Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) can produce analgesia, but its associated cortical, brainstem, and spinal response patterns in humans remain incompletely understood. To compare the analgesic effects and associated brain-spinal response patterns of two TENS protocols: high-frequency/low-intensity and low-frequency/high-intensity stimulation. Ninety-two healthy adults were randomized to high-frequency TENS, low-frequency TENS, or sham stimulation. Bilateral heat-pain responses were assessed using simultaneous brain-spinal functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) before and after a 30-min intervention. Pain ratings, regional activation, and periaqueductal gray (PAG)-centered functional connectivity were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models with correction for multiple comparisons. The two TENS protocols produced different spatial profiles of analgesia. High-frequency/low-intensity TENS produced treated-side analgesia relative to sham for pain intensity (β = -2.57, 95 % confidence interval [CI] [-3.26, -1.87]) and unpleasantness (β = -2.53, 95 % CI [-3.51, -1.55]). Treated-side analgesia was accompanied by reduced heat-evoked activity in the secondary somatosensory cortex (S2), PAG, rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM), and C6 spinal cord, increased ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) activity, and altered PAG-spinal connectivity. Low-frequency/high-intensity TENS produced bilateral analgesia, reducing pain intensity on the treated and untreated sides (β = -2.07 and -1.75, respectively) and unpleasantness (β = -1.98 and -1.70, respectively). This bilateral effect was accompanied by reduced activity in primary somatosensory cortex (S1)/dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC)/supplementary motor area (SMA), S2, and spinal cord, together with PAG-S1 and PAG-spinal connectivity changes. TENS analgesia was associated with protocol-specific brain-spinal response patterns. High-frequency/low-intensity TENS produced localized analgesia with neural changes consistent with spinal and supraspinal modulation, whereas low-frequency/high-intensity TENS produced bilateral analgesia with broader PAG-sensorimotor-spinal involvement.

title: FTO deficiency mediates ferroptosis to exacerbate cobalt-induced neurotoxicity.
abstract: Cobalt, a toxic environmental contaminant, has been implicated in human neurological damage. However, the detailed molecular basis of cobalt-triggered neurotoxicity remains poorly uncovered. In the present study, we elucidated the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) demethylase fat mass and obesity-associated protein (FTO) downregulation mediates the activation of ferroptosis to drive cobalt-triggered neurodegeneration. We established an in vitro model using H4 cells and an in vivo model using C57BL/6 mice. Animal experiments provided initial evidence underscoring the critical involvement of ferroptosis in cobalt-associated neurotoxicity. Furthermore, in vitro assays revealed that ferroptosis is triggered subsequent to oxidative stress induced by cobalt exposure. Notably, MeRIP-seq profiling of H4 cells and mouse cortex revealed that ferroptosis-associated genes exhibited differential m6A modification, suggesting m6A modification might be involved in modulating ferroptosis. Concurrently, Gene Ontology and KEGG enrichment analyses revealed that genes bearing differential m6A modifications were significantly clustered within pathways linked to ferroptosis as well as neurodegenerative diseases. Moreover, we found that FTO depletion effectively enhanced ferroptosis following cobalt-induced oxidative stress. Mechanistically, FTO depletion enhanced m6A modification of GPX4 and transferrin receptor protein 1 (TFRC) mRNAs, leading to reduced GPX4 and elevated TFRC expression, which aggravated cobalt-induced ferroptosis. More importantly, we observed that central nervous system specific knockout of Fto exacerbated cobalt-induced neurobehavioral deficits and neuropathological damage through ferroptosis activation. Collectively, these results provide important insights into cobalt-induced neurotoxicity by targeting FTO deficiency-mediated ferroptosis and offer an innovative strategy for investigating neurodegenerative processes driven by environmental toxicants.

title: Paclitaxel induces region-specific microglial remodeling associated with chronic behavioral deficits and modulated by electroacupuncture in rats.
abstract: Chemotherapy-associated behavioral deficits, including cognitive impairment and depression, collectively termed chemobrain, often persist into the chronic phase after treatment, yet their underlying cellular mechanisms remain unclear. In particular, it remains unknown whether long-lasting behavioral deficits are associated with sustained neuroinflammatory responses or other forms of microglial alteration. We therefore examined whether chronic behavioral deficits were associated with region-specific microglial morphological alterations and inflammatory gene expression changes, and how EA intervention was associated with these alterations. Male SD rats were assigned to the Control, PTX, and PTX + EA groups. Cognitive and emotional behaviors were assessed using behavioral tests. Microglial morphology in the hippocampus across the dorsoventral axis and mPFC was analyzed using skeleton analysis, and inflammatory gene expression was evaluated by qPCR. PTX induced cognitive impairment and depressive-like behavior, accompanied by a selective reduction in microglial process number and length in the dentate gyrus of the dorsal hippocampus and the infralimbic cortex of the mPFC. Microglial morphology differed between the PTX and PTX + EA groups in both regions, although the difference in the dorsal dentate gyrus was limited to process number. No significant changes in the inflammatory genes examined were detected in the hippocampus or mPFC. Thus, PTX produced chronic behavioral deficits accompanied by selective microglial remodeling in the dorsal dentate gyrus and infralimbic cortex, but not in the ventral hippocampus, with no detectable changes in inflammatory gene expression. Behavioral outcomes and microglial morphology differed between the PTX and PTX + EA groups, indicating an association between EA intervention and region-specific microglial remodeling.

title: The Effects of Blueberry Consumption on Cerebral Blood Flow and Brain Glutathione Levels in Older Adults: A Double-Blind Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial.
journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
abstract: Age-related declines in brain antioxidant capacity and cerebral blood flow (CBF) contribute to cognitive decline and increase the risk of Alzheimer's disease and dementias. Dietary approaches that enhance cerebral antioxidant defenses and CBF may promote brain health during aging. Blueberries are rich in polyphenols with antioxidant properties, and cardiometabolic and endothelial benefits, and may improve both brain glutathione (GSH), a major endogenous antioxidant, and CBF. However, the effects of blueberry intake on brain GSH and CBF have not been well established. To determine the effects of blueberry consumption on brain GSH and CBF in brain regions vulnerable to aging and neurodegeneration in older adults. In a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial, older adults aged 65-89 years with low berry intake (≤1 serving/week) consumed freeze-dried whole blueberry powder (hereafter "blueberry") equivalent to one cup of fresh blueberries or a matched placebo powder for three months. Brain GSH and regional CBF were measured using multiple quantum chemical shift imaging and pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling MRI, respectively. Sixty participants completed the intervention with adherence exceeding 92% in both groups. Blueberry powder consumption did not alter brain GSH concentrations compared with placebo but significantly increased CBF in the anterior cingulate cortex (P=0.03), a region involved in executive function and cognitive control. Within-group analyses showed increased CBF after blueberry consumption in the anterior cingulate cortex (7%, P=0.03; 95% confidence interval: 1.0%, 14.7%), caudate (7%, P=0.01; 2.9%, 15.8%), and putamen (6%, P=0.04; 0.3%, 13.9%), whereas no significant changes were observed in the placebo group. Compared with placebo, blueberry consumption increased CBF in the anterior cingulate cortex, a brain region relevant to age-related cognitive decline. No corresponding brain GSH changes were observed, suggesting that the effects of blueberry polyphenols are more consistent with vascular modulation than alterations in cerebral antioxidant status. NCT05024916 CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRY URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05024916.

title: Individualized structural brain network and transcriptomic characterization of heterogeneity in type 2 diabetes mellitus.
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a heterogeneous metabolic disorder that also affects the brain, yet prior neuroimaging studies have predominantly focused on group-level comparisons, obscuring interindividual variability in brain structural organization. To capture this heterogeneity, we constructed individualized differential structural covariance networks for 156 individuals with T2DM using 148 healthy controls as a normative reference. Unsupervised clustering based on these individualized networks revealed two neuroanatomical subtypes with distinct network configurations. Most subtype-differentiating edges showed higher values in one subtype, whereas a smaller set of edges, primarily involving the basal ganglia and cerebellum, showed higher values in the other. Integration with transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas identified genes spatially associated with subtype-related differences. These genes were enriched in processes including receptor tyrosine kinase signaling and glycerolipid metabolism, with preferential expression in the striatum and cerebellum. Together, these findings characterize interindividual variation in brain structural covariance in T2DM and identify candidate molecular processes associated with the observed subtype differences.

title: Establishment of an animal model of GPIAS-defined tinnitus-like behavior with normal auditory brainstem response threshold profiles.
abstract: Noise-induced tinnitus models can include hearing loss and other auditory changes that complicate interpretation of behavioral measures. We characterized a candidate exposure paradigm associated with GPIAS-defined tinnitus-like behavior and no significant day-14 ABR threshold differences from baseline. A normative cohort of 100 male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent repeated GPIAS testing to establish a criterion for GPIAS-defined tinnitus-like behavior. Separate cohorts were exposed bilaterally to 100-120 dB SPL white noise for 2 h and classified using the resulting 0.34 cutoff. ABR, DPOAEs, and cochlear immunofluorescence for CtBP2 presynaptic ribbons assessed auditory and morphological changes. Bilateral auditory measurements were averaged within each rat before analysis. On day 14, ABR thresholds did not differ significantly from baseline at 100 or 105 dB SPL but remained elevated at 12 kHz after 110 dB SPL, 8 kHz after 115 dB SPL, and all six frequencies after 120 dB SPL. Findings at 105 dB SPL included persistent GPIAS-defined tinnitus-like behavior, reduced day-14 wave-I amplitude at 8 kHz, and no evident outer hair cell loss. On day 14, the tinnitus subgroup showed smaller CtBP2-positive punctum areas and fewer puncta per inner hair cell than controls and the non-tinnitus subgroup. Bilateral exposure to 105 dB SPL white noise for 2 h provides a candidate paradigm associated with GPIAS-defined tinnitus-like behavior and auditory features consistent with hidden hearing loss, supporting further mechanistic and therapeutic studies relevant to tinnitus with normal conventional audiograms.

title: Neuroinformatics in Pakistan: building a national framework for data-driven Neuroscience and Neurotechnology.
abstract: Neuroinformatics represents a rapidly evolving interdisciplinary field that integrates Neuroscience, computational science, artificial intelligence, and data engineering to acquire, manage, analyze, and interpret increasingly complex brain data. Advances in Neuroimaging, electrophysiology, multimodal data integration, and computational Neuroscience have made robust Neuroinformatics infrastructure essential for modern data-driven Neuroscience, precision medicine, and intelligent clinical decision support. This Perspective examines the emerging Neuroinformatics landscape in Pakistan, examining institutional research capacity, computational infrastructure, educational and training initiatives, funding mechanisms, clinical informatics, and emerging Neurotechnology and industrial activities. Global developments in Neuroinformatics and Neurotechnology are also examined to contextualize Pakistan's current position and identify opportunities for strategic integration into the international Neuroscience ecosystem. Major barriers are critically evaluated, including fragmented neurological data resources, limited high-performance computing capacity, shortages of interdisciplinary expertise, regulatory and ethical challenges, inadequate interoperability, and barriers to sustained academic-clinical-industrial collaboration. Building on this evidence-informed assessment, this Perspective proposes a national strategy centered on interoperable Neurodata repositories, shared computational infrastructure, interdisciplinary workforce development, responsible data governance, strengthened research-industry partnerships, and international collaboration. Collectively, these priorities provide a practical roadmap for transforming existing computational and Neuroscience capabilities into a coordinated national Neuroinformatics ecosystem. Strategic investment in these areas could strengthen neurological research, accelerate data-driven clinical innovation, and position Pakistan as a more active contributor to the global Neuroinformatics and Neurotechnology landscape.

title: Rest-activity rhythm robustness and prospective mood symptoms in adolescence: Moderating effects of chronotype, sleep timing, and reward sensitivity.
abstract: Adolescence is a period of heightened bipolar spectrum disorder (BSD) risk involving changes in reward and circadian systems. Circadian disruptions can destabilize mood, and the impact may be more pronounced in individuals with trait vulnerabilities. We tested whether greater reward sensitivity or eveningness influenced the predictive association between rest-activity rhythm (RAR) disruption and dimensional mood symptoms relevant to BSD. Adolescents (N = 199) in a prospective BSD-risk study completed baseline measures of reward sensitivity, morningness-eveningness, mood symptoms, and one week of actigraphy to generate Circadian Function Index (CFI), a composite measure of RAR robustness. Mood measures were readministered six months later. Regression models tested interactions between reward sensitivity, morningness-eveningness, and sleep midpoint and CFI to predict hypo-/manic or depressive symptom severity at follow-up. CFI was not independently associated with mood symptoms. Morningness-eveningness (b = 0.59, p < .001) and sleep midpoint (b = -2.77, p = .013) significantly moderated the association between CFI and hypo-/manic symptoms. Sleep midpoint (b = -5.40, p = .023) and reward sensitivity (b = -1.32, p = .033) significantly moderated the association between CFI and depressive symptoms. The impact of CFI on mood symptoms depended upon vulnerabilities. Lower CFI predicted greater hypo-/manic symptoms among adolescents with greater eveningness and later sleep midpoint. Lower CFI predicted greater depressive symptoms among those with later sleep midpoint. Contrary to hypotheses, higher CFI predicted greater depressive symptoms for adolescents with reward hyposensitivity. These results highlight potential targets for future identification studies relevant to BSD.

title: Speech-based differentiation of unipolar and bipolar depression across scripted reading and interview questions.
abstract: Differentiating bipolar depression (BPD) from unipolar depression (UPD) remains clinically challenging. We examined whether acoustic and linguistic speech features could support this distinction and whether their informativeness varied across scripted reading and interview questions. This study included 109 healthy controls (HCs), 52 patients with UPD, and 53 patients with BPD experiencing depressive episodes. Participants completed a scripted reading task and an interview-based speech task comprising 16 questions. Acoustic features were extracted from all audio recordings, and linguistic features were derived from interview transcripts. Group differences were examined using robust analysis of covariance with global false discovery rate correction. Two-level stacking models with fold-wise sex adjustment of acoustic features evaluated classification performance and importance of speech features and interview-based speech elicitation prompts. Multiple acoustic and linguistic features showed significant group differences in interview responses, whereas no acoustic features differed significantly during scripted reading. The best-performing models achieved F1 scores of 0.6655 for three-class classification (HC, UPD and BPD) and 0.6430 for binary classification (UPD and BPD). Within interview-based speech, statistical and machine learning analyses identified Average Pause Duration, Phonation Ratio, and quantity-related expressions as particularly informative features. Two interview questions about (hypo-)manic experiences contributed most to differentiating BPD from UPD. Acoustic and linguistic speech features may help differentiate BPD from UPD during depressive episodes, with their informativeness varying across speech tasks and interview questions. Our findings suggest that targeted interview-based speech assessment may have potential as a non-invasive adjunct to conventional clinical evaluation.

title: De-identification of health data for open sharing: A scoping review.
abstract: Open science and data sharing initiatives are increasingly shaping health research by promoting transparency and collaboration. However, sharing health data introduces privacy risks, requiring robust de-identification methods. Previous reviews have largely focused on specific data types, with limited synthesis across diverse and multimodal health data. This scoping review mapped de-identification methods across health data modalities and identified common techniques, tools, challenges, and gaps. We conducted a scoping review guided by the Arksey and O'Malley framework, with enhancements from Levac et al. and the Joanna Briggs Institute. Searches of MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Web of Science identified 2434 documents. After duplicate removal, 2384 documents underwent full-text screening. Data was charted using an iteratively refined extraction tool capturing study characteristics, de-identification methods, data modalities, evaluation approaches, and reported outcomes. Quantitative and inductive content analyses were conducted. A total of 309 documents met inclusion criteria. Most focused on unstructured data (n = 91, 29.4 %), structured data (n = 86, 27.8 %), or medical images (n = 67, 21.7 %). Single-modality data were addressed in 88.7 % of documents (n = 274), while 11.3 % (n = 35) addressed multimodal data. Hybrid approaches combining multiple techniques were more common (n = 173, 56.0 %) than single-method approaches (n = 136, 44.0 %). Most methods were developed in academic or research settings (n = 262, 84.8 %), with limited clinical implementation (n = 19, 6.1 %). Patient/public involvement was rare (n = 14, 4.5 %). Common author-reported challenges included preserving data utility, scalability, and inconsistent reporting standards. Findings highlight the need for modality-specific evaluation frameworks and standardized reporting to support trustworthy, privacy-preserving health data sharing.

title: Engineering human brain microphysiological systems for alzheimer's disease (AD) and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) modeling and drug testing: translational promise, limitations, and future directions.
abstract: This review examines the emerging role of human brain microphysiological systems (HBMPS) in recapitulating diseases and evaluating their translational potential and limitations for Alzheimer's disease (AD) and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Both disorders differ in underlying cause, but converge on shared downstream pathophysiology such as tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction. We review the critical pathophysiological features relevant to modeling AD and CTE and introduce HBMPS platforms/validation strategies as potential tools for evaluating therapeutic compounds as well as drug-delivery approaches. We also provide a systematic comparison of the relative advantages and disadvantages of 2D, HBMPS, Xenograft, and animal models and discuss the future potential of HBMPS's drug-testing platform. We further discuss current challenges of HBMPS related to drug testing, engineering extracellular matrix for tissue chips, and BBB penetration in AD and CTE. We suggest future integration of organoid xenografts and AI-assisted frameworks to enhance pathophysiological fidelity/drug predictive capability and to bridge the gap between HBMPS and animal models. In summary, this paper reviews HBMPS technologies as future translation platforms' direction for drug screening and delivery, while providing current limitations and challenges including model validation, reproducibility, and standardized regulatory bases required for preclinical success for HBMPS use. Rather than comparing biological complexity with translational validity, this review applies a decision-oriented framework that distinguishes mechanistic fidelity, comparative candidate ranking, predictive validation, investigational new drug (IND)-supporting use, and replacement of a defined animal test. For each use, we identify quantitative transport, exposure-response, pharmacodynamic, safety, and reproducibility evidence required to support an advance, redesign, or go/stop decision.

title: Dopaminergic Neurotoxicity Induces Parkinsonian-Like Phenotypes in Daphnia magna.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is associated with dopaminergic neurodegeneration, in which mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress play central roles. However, environmentally relevant invertebrate models for studying dopaminergic neurotoxicity remain limited. Here, we developed a Parkinsonism-like model in Daphnia magna using sublethal exposures to the prototypical dopaminergic neurotoxicant MPTP [1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine] and the environmentally relevant pesticide rotenone. Both compounds induced concentration-dependent increases in reactive oxygen species, marked depletion of dopamine and related metabolites in the head, and a strong downregulation of key dopaminergic genes, indicating profound disruption of dopaminergic homeostasis and redox balance and providing evidence consistent with construct validity. These molecular alterations were accompanied by functional alterations consistent with face validity, including reduced hopping distance, increased low-locomotion states, impaired photomotor responses and habituation, altered phototaxis and colour preference, particularly after MPTP exposure, and reduced heart rate. Together, these findings support the potential utility of D. magna as a sensitive, integrative, and ecologically relevant model for investigating dopaminergic neurotoxicity and Parkinsonism-related adverse outcome pathways triggered by environmental chemicals.

title: Dyadic fNIRS Hyperscanning: Experimental Paradigms and What They Reveal About Interbrain Synchrony.
abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning enables the simultaneous measurement of the brain activities of various individuals performing shared or interactive tasks and estimating their interbrain synchrony (IBS). IBS is believed to reflect different mechanisms, including social bonding or mutual prediction, and to be modulated by various factors, such as familiarity or the experimental paradigm. In this systematic review, we assessed fNIRS hyperscanning studies conducted until January 2026, focusing on the experimental protocols and their relation to reported IBS findings. Specifically, we aimed to understand task dependence of IBS results and how they differ between different kinds of dyad compositions. Additionally, we investigated other parameters, including IBS metrics and the association between IBS and psychological, behavioral, and physiological measures. We reviewed a total of 206 studies, revealing a predominance of joint action task paradigms. Our findings suggest that IBS is modulated by the characteristics of dyad composition. IBS is usually higher in dyads with closer bonds, and varies with gender, although a universal pattern could not be identified. Furthermore, the study protocols employed also seem to have an influence on IBS, as participants who engage in face-to-face interactions frequently show higher IBS than those who do not. We also observed that IBS is often associated with behavioral and psychological outcomes, while the association with physiological outcomes is scarcely studied. Future research should consistently include details about dyad familiarity and sex pairings, expand to underrepresented dyads, and investigate IBS across diverse paradigms and contexts in association with other metrics.

title: Dihydrocaffeic acid alleviates APOE4-associated astrocyte dysfunction and cognitive impairment via LRP1/p38 MAPK signaling.
abstract: Dihydrocaffeic acid (DHCA) is a phenolic acid produced through the microbial metabolism of plant-derived caffeoylquinic acids. DHCA has been detected in human plasma following oral administration of a standardized aqueous extract of Centella asiatica (L.) Urb., a medicinal plant traditionally used to improve memory and cognitive function. However, whether DHCA exerts neuroprotective effects against APOE4-associated Alzheimer's disease-like pathology remains unclear. To investigate whether DHCA ameliorates APOE4-associated cognitive deficits and neuropathological abnormalities and to assess the role of astrocytic LRP1/p38 MAPK signaling. Twelve-month-old APOE4 mice were administered DHCA once daily for 21 days, with age-matched APOE3 mice and vehicle-treated APOE4 mice serving as controls. Cognitive function, Alzheimer's disease-related neuropathology, neuronal and synaptic integrity, astrocyte phenotypes, and lipid metabolism were evaluated. Mechanistic studies were performed in APOE4-overexpressing U251 cells using siRNA-mediated LRP1 knockdown and pharmacological activation of p38 MAPK. DHCA improved object recognition and spatial learning and memory, reduced amyloid deposition and tau phosphorylation, restored neuronal and synaptic markers, shifted astrocyte-reactivity markers toward a neuroprotective profile, and restored proteins involved in lipid metabolism. DHCA also increased LRP1 expression and reduced p38 MAPK phosphorylation. LRP1 knockdown or p38 MAPK activation partially reversed these cellular effects. DHCA ameliorated APOE4-associated cognitive deficits and neuropathological alterations, at least partly through modulation of LRP1/p38 MAPK-related signaling in the APOE4-overexpressing U251 model, astrocyte reactivity, and lipid metabolism. These findings identify DHCA as a potential neuroprotective metabolite derived from plant polyphenols.

title: Neuro-XR Primer: Blending Neuroscience and Extended Reality to Facilitate Cognitive Investigation.
abstract: Neuro-XR refers to the amalgamation of neuroimaging and extended reality (XR) including augmented, mixed and virtual reality. Both sets of technology have developed rapidly and in isolation, and here, we show that they have great potential when combined. Mobile neuroimaging technology is becoming increasingly available, offering researchers greater flexibility. Similarly, XR devices are now affordable and lightweight and can be coupled with open-source software for developing experiments. We are now at a time where neuroimaging and XR are paired to investigate new cognitive questions but also to replicate seminal research. Neuro-XR provides cognitive neuroscience and XR-based applications such as medicine, quantitative understanding (through behaviour and neural data) and analysis of real-time interactions. In this primer, we introduce the term 'Neuro-XR' and define the scope of the technique through a concept-driven synthesis based on the literature and driven by the authors' expertise. More generally, we discuss the current research in the field and explore some potential future applications. Finally, we provide suggestions and guidance for practising Neuro-XR based on our combined experience across these modalities.

title: Transforming suicide helpline services into resilient global health infrastructure.
Geometric inference of cross-species transcriptome correspondence.
abstract: Sequence homology reveals evolutionary gene correspondences, but identifying functionally corresponding genes within specific cell types or during cell fate specification remains non-trivial. Here, frameworks that translate insights from model organisms into other species would accelerate wet-lab studies, so we develop Species-OT, a cross-species transcriptome analysis framework using Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport, which quantitatively compares the geometry of transcriptome distributions. Given a pair of bulk or single-cell RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) datasets, Species-OT returns a gene-to-gene correspondence capturing probabilistic alignments of regulatory roles and a transcriptomic distance quantifying overall divergence. Applied pairwise, Species-OT yields a transcriptomic discrepancy array and a hierarchical clustering tree analogous to a phylogenetic tree. We validate Species-OT using bulk RNA-seq data for cell fate specification from pluripotent stem cells in mice, monkeys, and humans and single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) data from pluripotent stem cells of six mammalian species. Species-OT identifies gene correspondences within cell fate specification, while transcriptomic discrepancies recapitulate expected species relationships.

title: EPCR expression marks CD150neg deeply dormant long-term hematopoietic stem cells.
abstract: Cell surface expression of the Slam family member CD150 is widely used for the prospective isolation of multipotent long-term hematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSCs). Here, we identify a bona fide endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR)+CD150- HSC subset, termed LT-HSC2, that sustains serial multi-lineage reconstitution. Long-term label-retaining assays reveal that LT-HSC2s are more deeply dormant than conventional EPCR+CD150+ LT-HSC1s, exhibit reduced cell cycle activation in response to inflammatory stress, and preserve stemness for prolonged periods in vivo. Moreover, combining EPCR with established HSC and multipotent progenitor (MPP) markers resolves the earliest stages of lineage divergence toward megakaryocytic/erythroid-biased CD150+ and lymphoid-biased CD150- trajectories. Thus, EPCR expression in HSCs and MPPs is associated with increased stemness, whereas CD150 expression does not encompass the full spectrum of long-term repopulating HSCs. Our findings establish EPCR+CD150- LT-HSC2s as a distinct, exceptionally dormant stem-cell subset and reveal an additional layer of HSC heterogeneity governing self-renewal, decreased stress sensitvity. and earliest lineage priming.

title: Organoids and organs-on-a-chip as new approach methodologies at the convergence of cell biology and bioengineering.
abstract: The rapid growth of new approach methodologies (NAMs), including organoids and organs-on-a-chip (OOCs), has revealed a need for interdisciplinary dialogue between cell biologists and bioengineers to develop human models that can best complement therapeutic development. Stem cell-derived and bioengineered human tissue models are redefining how we understand human physiology and pathophysiology, offering control that traditional preclinical models cannot provide. By recapitulating complex tissue microenvironments, multi-organ interactions, and patient-specific biology, these systems are bridging long-standing gaps in the drug development and clinical application pipelines. Here, we synthesize advances in organoids, OOCs, and other bioengineered technologies for translational medicine to identify remaining gaps, including challenges in reproducibility, validation, and regulatory acceptance. Emerging opportunities at the intersection of synthetic biology, multi-omics, machine learning, and genetic engineering are positioning NAMs not merely as improved experimental tools but as foundational platforms for accelerating therapeutic discovery and enabling personalized medicine at scale.

title: Multimodal spatial transcriptomics redefines cortical pathology in Huntington's disease.
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is caused by CAG expansion in the huntingtin gene (HTT), yet how somatic repeat instability and HTT inclusions relate to selective cell loss in the human brain remains unclear. We have developed a multimodal spatial transcriptomics approach that enables the definition of transcriptional programs with subcellular resolution, somatic CAG repeat lengths, and eight other pathology markers, including HTT inclusions, in every cell of intact brain sections. Imaging 428,173 cells in the control and HD cortex revealed the selective vulnerability of layer 5-6 (L5-6) near-projecting (NP) neurons and L6b deep-layer excitatory neurons, which undergo a >50% loss that is closely linked to large somatic repeat expansions (>450 ± 55 CAGs). Intranuclear inclusions were most prevalent at intermediate somatic repeat expansions (250-350 CAGs) and were associated with broader transcriptional changes than somatic repeat expansion alone. These data provide a comprehensive resource and establish a general framework for connecting repeat expansion and protein pathology across diverse cell types.

title: Somatic DNA-repeat expansions initiate distinct yet analogous changes in Huntington's disease cortical and striatal neurons.
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) affects the neocortex and striatum with different timing, severity, and gene-expression changes. These pathologies have long been proposed to involve different pathogenic mechanisms, with one brain area's degeneration leading to the other's. Striatal neurons degenerate in HD as their huntingtin (HTT) CAG-repeat tracts expand somatically beyond 150 CAGs. Here, we find that cortical pyramidal neurons in HD undergo biological changes analogous to those in striatal neurons-the same sequence of pathological phases, with toxicity also commencing at ∼150 CAGs but then changing their gene expression in distinct ways. Pyramidal neurons' precise molecular identities, rather than their areal or laminar locations, appeared to determine the extent of this somatic DNA-repeat expansion, which varied up to 20-fold among pyramidal neuron subtypes. Cortical and striatal neurons also shared a key pathological feature: nuclear inclusions of aggregated HTT protein in those nuclei with expansions well beyond 150 CAGs.

title: The characteristics of perivascular proinflammation in 4-repeat tauopathies.
abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and corticobasal degeneration (CBD) are both neurodegenerative diseases characterized by aggregates composed of 4-repeat (4R) tau protein. They have distinct neuropathological features and classic clinical symptoms; however, the signs and symptoms overlap across the two syndromes. Accumulating evidence suggests that dysregulated immune response is a major contributing factor to neurodegeneration but its role in 4R-tauopathies remains undetermined. The aim is to explore the involvement of neuroinflammation from a vascular perspective in 4R-tauopathies. Autopsies from four controls, three PSP, and three CBD cases were assessed. Samples were obtained from the superior/middle frontal gyrus (S/M-FG) and basal ganglia (BG). Immunofluorescence staining included neuroinflammatory markers: glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1 (Iba1), cluster of differentiation 68 (CD68); vascular markers: collagen type IV (ColIV), monocarboxylate transporter-1 (MCT1), and α-smooth muscle actin (αSMA). Maximally projected confocal z-stack images of vasculature were used as a mask to quantify total perivascular GFAP+/Iba1+/CD68+ labeling. GFAP immunoreactivity ratio between MCT1 and αSMA double labeled arteries and veins was quantified to further differentiate venular and arteriolar involvement into proinflammatory activation. Both PSP and CBD had widespread perivascular proinflammatory changes, although greater in CBD. The activated GFAP+ astrocytes and microglia/macrophages in CBD were distributed extensively in S/M-FG and BG, with S/M-FG WM more affected. In PSP, abundant neuroinflammation was found in BG. The involvement of vasculature type was distinct among the two 4R-tauopathies, while CBD showed comparable proinflammatory changes in arterioles and venules, PSP exhibited predominant proinflammation in venules. The regional pattern of perivascular proinflammation differed between PSP and CBD, corresponding to the characteristic affected brain regions. CBD had more severe perivascular proinflammation that involved both arterioles and venules, while venules were more affected in PSP. Perivascular proinflammation may be a critical pathophysiological process in 4R-tauopathies.

title: Diet quality, gut microbiome diversity, and clinical disability in multiple sclerosis: A cross-sectional case-control study.
abstract: Dietary patterns and gut microbiome composition are increasingly recognised as modifiable factors in multiple sclerosis (MS). We aimed to evaluate dietary quality, microbiome diversity, and their inter-relationships with MS status, clinical disability, and disease-modifying therapy (DMT). We compared 288 MS cases with 274 household healthy controls (HHC). Dietary intake was assessed using healthy eating index (HEI-2015), and the groups were compared and associations analysed using multivariable linear regression. Among all HEI-2015 components, only total fruit intake was significantly higher in MS (β=+0.46; 95% CI: +0.19 to +0.74; FDR q = 0.014). Higher HEI-2015 scores were positively associated with greater Shannon alpha diversity (β=+0.077/10-unit increment; 95% CI: +0.003 to +0.150; p = 0.042). The PERMANOVA revealed independent association between microbiome beta diversity and smoking (R²=0.011; p = 0.007), BMI (R²=0.007; p = 0.010), age (R²=0.006; p = 0.027), and MS status (R²=0.005; p = 0.026), but not with diet quality (R²=0.006; p = 0.171). The whole grains consumption was directly associated with EDSS (FDR q = 0.033). Microbial richness differed across DMT categories (p = 0.001), and mechanism-level analysis attributed this to natalizumab, anti-CD20 therapy and dimethyl fumarate. In conclusion, higher fruit intake and dietary quality positively were related to gut microbiome diversity in MS. Disease status, smoking, and BMI are the primary drivers of microbiome community composition. Therefore, dietary modification could be a potential adjunctive strategy in MS management.

title: Selective expression and neurochemical characterization of Huntingtin-associated protein 1-expressing neurons in the adult mouse habenula.
abstract: Huntingtin-associated protein 1 (HAP1) is a neuroprotective interactor with pathogenic proteins implicated in several neurodegenerative diseases. The habenula is a small epithalamic structure that has emerged as a critical regulator of aversion, reward, stress responses, anxiety, and mood. Despite its pivotal roles in intracellular trafficking and neuronal function, the distribution and neurochemical characterization of HAP1 within the habenula have not been systematically investigated. Therefore, the present study used Western blotting and immunohistochemistry to characterize HAP1 immunoreactivity in the adult mouse habenula. Our current study revealed that HAP1-immunoreactive (ir) neurons were selectively localized to the lateral habenula (LHb), whereas no detectable HAP1 immunoreactivity was observed in the medial habenula. Within the LHb, HAP1-ir neurons were concentrated in the LHbMC, LHbMPc, and LHbMS subdivisions. Double-label immunofluorescence revealed that 9% of HAP1-positive neurons expressed choline acetyltransferase and 22% expressed neuronal nitric oxide synthase. Moderate proportions expressed calbindin (52%) and calretinin (59%), whereas the highest proportions expressed calcitonin gene-related peptide (84%) and cholecystokinin (74%). No detectable co-localization was observed between HAP1 and parvalbumin. Substance P immunoreactivity was observed in fibers rather than neuronal somata within the analyzed LHb region, precluding quantitative assessment of neuronal co-expression. These findings demonstrate that HAP1-ir neurons exhibit distinct neurochemical profiles, particularly involving peptidergic and calcium-binding protein-expressing neuronal populations. These selective co-expression profiles highlight the neurochemical heterogeneity of HAP1-ir neurons within the LHb and provide an anatomical framework for future investigations of HAP1 function in habenular circuitry.

title: Advances in cartilage tissue engineering: Strategies, challenges, and future directions.
abstract: Articular cartilage is highly susceptible to physical and degenerative damage due to its avascular nature and limited regenerative capacity. The aim of this review article is to explore recent advances in cartilage tissue engineering to develop alternative therapeutic approaches for repairing damaged tissues. A structured search was conducted across scientific databases-including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science-to identify relevant studies published between 2000 and 2026 regarding cartilage tissue engineering. The search covered topics such as cell sources, biomaterial scaffolds, growth factors, bioreactor systems, and emerging cartilage regeneration strategies, utilizing a combination of keywords and terms related to cartilage tissue engineering, cartilage regeneration, biomaterials, scaffolds, hydrogels, stem cells, chondrogenesis, and 3D bioprinting. Retrieved studies were screened for relevance to the review's scope, and eligible studies were qualitatively analyzed and synthesized to summarize recent advancements, existing challenges, and future directions in the field of cartilage tissue engineering. As this study was designed as a narrative review, no formal meta-analysis or quantitative statistical synthesis was performed. The findings indicate that the use of mesenchymal stem cells, nanostructured scaffolds with bioactive compositions, and the application of mechanical and chemical factors play a significant role in cell differentiation into chondrocytes and successful cartilage regeneration. However, challenges such as mechanical integrity, long-term durability, and clinical translation still remain. Cartilage tissue engineering holds great potential for the treatment of cartilage injuries; nevertheless, further studies are needed to optimize cell sources, scaffold design, and environmental control conditions in the tissue engineering process to achieve effective clinical applications.

title: Aloysia deserticola (rica-rica) essential oil impairs inhibitory synaptic transmission in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons.
abstract: Aloysia deserticola is an aromatic plant native to the Chilean Andean highlands that has traditionally been used in herbal preparations. Although a previous behavioral study reported the anxiolytic and antidepressant-like effects of rica-rica essential oil in an animal model, its neurophysiological actions at cellular and synaptic levels remain largely unexplored. In this study, we characterized A. deserticola essential oil (AD-EO) using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and examined its acute effects on GABAergic synaptic transmission via whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from CA1 pyramidal neurons in acute dorsal hippocampal slices obtained from C57BL/6 J mice. GC-MS analysis revealed an enriched thujone chemical profile, with peaks tentatively identified as α- and β-thujone accounting for 89.06% and 3.38% of the total chromatographic area, respectively. Application of AD-EO to the bath reduced evoked inhibitory postsynaptic current (eIPSC) amplitude in a concentration-dependent manner and shortened eIPSC decay kinetics. This is consistent with a postsynaptic contribution to the suppression of inhibitory signaling. At intermediate-to-high estimated thujone-equivalent concentrations, AD-EO increased the paired-pulse ratio. Coefficient-of-variation analysis supported the presence of an additional presynaptic component. Consistent with these findings, AD-EO reduced the frequency and amplitude of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents. Furthermore, the effects on eIPSC amplitude and the paired-pulse ratio were reversible following washout. Together, these results demonstrate that AD-EO suppresses inhibitory synapses in CA1 pyramidal neurons via effects consistent with pre- and postsynaptic locus. These results provide electrophysiological evidence that AD-EO modulates hippocampal inhibitory transmission and support further investigation of the mechanisms underlying the neurophysiological actions of this complex natural preparation.

title: Reality stabilization: a unified framework for psychosis and post-psychotic depression.
abstract: Both quantum mechanics and cognitive neuroscience challenge the classical view of a passively perceived reality. Instead, they suggest that reality arises through a process of selection and stabilization from a field of possibilities. This article proposes that this "reality stabilization" framework can unify our understanding of psychosis and post-psychotic depression-two conditions that are currently studied as distinct phenomena, and which existing models of predictive coding, dopaminergic dysregulation, and network neuroscience rarely integrate into a single account. We conceptualize psychosis as a failure of neurocognitive decoherence, in which competing perceptual and interpretative states cannot be reduced to a single, coherent reality. Post-psychotic depression, in contrast, is framed as a compensatory hyperstabilization, in which a rigid, negatively valenced reality is restored, possibly mediated by altered DMN activity. The framework suggests that effective intervention must move beyond dopaminergic blockade to include strategies that promote adaptive network coherence and cognitive integration. The model remains hypothetical, and direct empirical evidence for decoherence-like processes, network changes, and the proposed temporal progression is limited. Future work should focus on empirical testing of stabilization and hyperstabilization mechanisms, longitudinal assessment across illness stages, and their possible therapeutic relevance.

title: Resistance training volume for major depressive disorder: the MoveMind randomized controlled trial protocol.
abstract: This randomized controlled trial aims to investigate the effects of resistance training (RT) volume (high vs. low) and non-exercise group on depressive symptoms, remission rates, adherence and the psychological and neurobiological mechanisms underlying these effects in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). A total of 150 adults (18-59 years) diagnosed with MDD will be randomized into three groups: high-volume RT (HV, n=50; 4 sets of 10-12 repetition maximum [RM]), low-volume RT (LV, n=50; 2 sets of 10-12 RM), and a non-exercise control group (CG, n=50). Participants in the intervention groups will train three non-consecutive days per week for 8 weeks. The primary outcome, depressive symptoms, will be assessed by a psychiatrist using the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale. Secondary outcomes will include potential psychological mechanisms (perceived self-efficacy, affective responses to exercise, and well-being), assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and at the 3-month follow-up, and neurobiological mechanisms assessed by inflammatory and metabolic biomarkers related to MDD pathophysiology, including TNF-α, IL-6, IL-10, IL-1β, CRP, IGF-1, BDNF, insulin, glucose, and cortisol, measured before and after the intervention. Tertiary outcomes will include dietary intake and ultra-processed food consumption (24-hour dietary recall), body composition (DXA), muscular strength, and sleep quality. Intervention efficacy will be analyzed using intention-to-treat linear mixed-effects models. The findings may contribute to more effective, personalized, and sustainable RT prescriptions that improve adherence and complement conventional treatments for MDD. https://ensaiosclinicos.gov.br/rg/, identifier RBR-9tn4ncp.

title: The HALF-IT score: proposing a simplified mechanical thrombectomy triage tool for basilar artery occlusion.
abstract: Basilar artery occlusion (BAO) is a devastating subtype of stroke with poor prognosis. Current patient selection tools for endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) are multi-tiered with interrater variability and limited validation studies. The HALF-IT score is a novel, simplified, dichotomized triaging tool focusing solely on the brainstem level. This study investigated the utility of the HALF-IT score to predict functional outcomes of EVT in patients with BAO. We conducted a multicenter, retrospective, cohort study including patients with acute BAO presenting to four comprehensive stroke centers between 2021-2025. Acute infarction of ≥50% of any brainstem section on any axial or coronal slice of MRI was considered HALF-IT positive, whereas < 50% was considered HALF-IT negative. The primary efficacy outcome was a favorable functional outcome, defined as a modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 0-3 at 90 days; functional independence (mRS 0-2) was analyzed as a secondary outcome. Reperfusion was graded with the modified Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction (mTICI) scale. Primary safety endpoints included symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage at 24 h and all-cause mortality at 90 days. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify independent predictors of the primary efficacy outcome. 37 patients (23 HALF-IT negative; 14 HALF-IT positive) met the inclusion criteria. The rate of 90-day mRS 0-3 was significantly lower in the HALF-IT positive compared with HALF-IT negative group [14.3% vs. 68.2%, OR 0.08 (0.01-0.45), p = 0.004]. HALF-IT positive status remained associated with a lower rate of 90-day mRS 0-3 after adjusting for age, initial NIHSS, onset-to-reperfusion time, intravenous thrombolysis administration complete reperfusion (final mTICI 3) [adjusted OR 0.02, 95% CI 0-0.84, p = 0.02]. Safety events were numerically higher in the HALF-IT positive group but the difference did not reach statistical significance. The two groups differed substantially at baseline in age, presenting NIHSS, and intravenous thrombolysis exposure, whereas stroke etiology (p = 0.28) and level of basilar occlusion (p = 0.63) were similarly distributed. In this small, retrospective, hypothesis-generating cohort, HALF-IT positivity was associated with worse 90-day functional outcomes after EVT for BAO. Further prospective validation in larger cohorts is required before the score can inform treatment decisions.

title: Dynamic Changes of Glu and Asp Concentrations in Blood and Spinal Fluid of Patients with Traumatic Spinal Cord Injury and Their Correlation with Prognosis.
abstract: As excitatory neurotransmitters, glutamic acid (Glu) and aspartic acid (Asp) may play a key role in the pathological process of traumatic spinal cord injury. The purpose of this study was to investigate the dynamic changes of Glu and Asp concentrations in blood and spinal fluid of patients with secondary spinal cord injury and their correlation with prognosis, so as to provide evidence for disease monitoring and treatment. In this study, 62 patients with secondary spinal cord injury admitted from January 2021 to December 2023 were selected as study subjects. Blood and spinal fluid samples were collected at 1, 3, 7, 14, and 28 days after injury, and the concentrations of Glu and Asp were determined by high-performance liquid chromatography. At the same time, the neurological functions of the patients at admission and 3 months after injury were evaluated using the American Spinal Cord Injury Association (ASIA) scoring criteria, and the patients were divided into a good prognosis group (ASIA score increased by ≥10 points) and a poor prognosis group (ASIA score increased by <10 points). Repeated measurement ANOVA was used to compare the differences of Glu and Asp concentrations in blood and spinal fluid of patients and the control group at different time points, and Spearman correlation analysis was used to explore the correlation between Glu and Asp concentrations and changes in ASIA score. Logistic regression analysis was performed to determine the risk factors affecting the prognosis of patients, and a receiver operating characteristics (ROC) curve was drawn to evaluate the diagnostic value of relevant indicators for prognosis. The concentrations of Glu and Asp in blood and spinal fluid of patients with poor prognosis were higher than those of patients with good prognosis at all time points (p < 0.05). The concentrations of Glu and Asp in blood and spinal fluid of patients with poor prognosis were higher than those of patients with good prognosis at all time points (p < 0.05). Spearman correlation analysis showed that Glu and Asp concentrations in blood and spinal fluid were significantly negatively correlated with ASIA score (r = -0.65, p < 0.01; r = -0.58, p < 0.01). Logistic regression analysis showed that Glu concentration (OR = 2.58, 95% CI: 1.56-4.29) and Asp concentration (OR = 2.25, 95% CI: 1.32-3.84) in spinal fluid 7 days after injury were independent risk factors for prognosis. ROC curve showed that the area under the curve of the combined detection of Glu and Asp in spinal fluid at 7 days after injury was significantly higher than that of single index (p < 0.01). The concentrations of Glu and Asp in the blood and spinal fluid of patients with acute traumatic spinal cord injury increase first and then decrease, and are closely related to the prognosis of patients. Early monitoring of these neurotransmitter concentrations after injury is helpful to evaluate the prognosis of patients and provide a reference for the formulation of personalized treatment plans. ROC curve analysis further clarified the diagnostic efficacy of relevant indicators in prognostic judgment.

title: Effects of Continuous and Intermittent Social Contact on the Welfare of Laboratory Rhesus Macaques (Macaca mulatta).
abstract: This study evaluated the effects of continuous full-contact (CFC) versus intermittent contact (IC) housing on the welfare of adult female rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) in a laboratory breeding colony. Twenty-four females from the California National Primate Research Center Time Mate Breeding Colony were assigned to CFC pairs with uninterrupted social access or to IC pairs separated for approximately 18 h daily. Behavioral observations collected over 5 months quantified affiliative, aggressive, anxious, and abnormal behaviors. Across the full day, macaques in CFC pairs exhibited higher rates of affiliative behavior than those in IC housing. IC pairs showed marked increases in abnormal behavior during separation periods, while the association between separation and anxiety-related behavior varied according to cage level. Analyses accounting for social contact availability indicated that increased abnormal behavior was specifically associated with periods of single housing. In contrast, no behavioral differences between housing groups were detected when both groups were observed under equivalent full-contact conditions. Aggressive behavior was more frequent in bottom-tier than top-tier cages, indicating that cage location may influence behavioral outcomes. Importantly, successful conception in females housed in CFC suggests that routine reproductive monitoring remained feasible under continuous full-contact housing conditions. These findings indicate that housing conditions providing continuous access to a social partner are associated with improved welfare compared to regimes that include repeated daily separation and suggest that routine separation practices may warrant reevaluation. Where feasible, CFC housing should be considered the preferred social housing strategy for laboratory rhesus macaques.

title: Diagnostic drivers of psychiatric inpatient bed use in Ireland 2013-2023: implications for service planning.
abstract: Psychiatric inpatient care is a high-resource component of mental health systems. Understanding the diagnoses driving inpatient care is essential for evidence-based service planning. This study describes psychiatric inpatient bed use in Ireland from 2013 to 2023 by diagnosis, sex, and age group. National descriptive analyses using aggregated data from the National Psychiatric Inpatient Reporting System, covering acute inpatient admissions in Ireland. The outcome was total number of inpatient bed days, categorised by ICD-10 diagnostic group. Primary analyses focused on public services, with private services reported separately. We additionally report on child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS), adult services, and sex-stratified results. Between 2013 and 2023, there were k=3,993,628 public and k=1,879,877 private inpatient bed days. In public services, schizophrenia spectrum disorders accounted for 41.9% of bed days (k=1,673,529), more than twice as many as the next most prevalent diagnosis. Men accounted for 51.2% of acute public bed days. In private adult services, depressive disorders accounted for the largest proportion of bed days (28.5%, k=513,166). In public and private CAMHS, eating disorders accounted for the largest proportion of bed days (25.6%, k=46,850 and 24.4%, k=18,775), respectively. This national analysis demonstrates that schizophrenia spectrum disorders represent, by far, the largest diagnostic group, accounting for 42% of public acute psychiatric inpatient beds days, highlighting the sustained, intensive service demands associated with these disorders. These data provide a clear empirical basis for future service planning, highlighting where targeted enhancements to community-based care could most effectively reduce the need for hospitalisation.
