title: Exploring the Integration of Trauma- and Violence-Informed Research Principles in Longitudinal Youth Mental Health Research: An Arts-Based Protocol.
journal: Health expectations : an international journal of public participation in health care and health policy
abstract: Youths' engagement and participation experiences within quantitative, longitudinal mental health studies remain underexplored. Youth with complex mental health needs have unique research participation experiences, underscoring the need for research approaches that strengthen relationality, trust, and engagement. Trauma- and violence-informed research (TVIR) principles offer a promising framework to address these challenges; however, youth-centred perspectives on how TVIR is operationalized within longitudinal mental health research remains limited. CALM STORY will explore youths' perspectives and experiences of participating in longitudinal quantitative mental health research that is grounded in TVIR principles, with attention to choice, collaboration, connection, and control. This protocol outlines CALM STORY, a qualitative, arts-based longitudinal evaluation of youth participation in the Cohort Network of AdoLescents and youth with Multiple mental health conditions (CALM) Master Observational Trial (MOT). CALM STORY is theoretically organised around both TVIR principles as well as the Lundy Model of Participation. We are purposefully sampling 30 youth aged 11-19 years enroled in the CALM MOT. Youth are completing two semi-structured qualitative interviews and a PhotoVoice workshop series. With consent, we will extract key socio-demographic data from the CALM MOT to contextualise TVIR strategies. Data will be managed using NVivo software and thematically analysed using a framework-based analytic approach guided by TVIR principles and the Lundy Model of participation. CALM STORY will generate youth-centred insights into TVIR engagement and participation in longitudinal quantitative mental health research. Findings will inform key deliverables, including the development and scaling TVIR training for research teams, as well as a research policy brief to be disseminated to the CALM MOT network, research ethics boards, and research funders. A Youth Advisory Group (YAG) comprised of youth with lived experience of multiple mental health conditions was established to consult on the CALM MOT's design, data collection, knowledge mobilisation, and sub-studies. The YAG informed CALM STORY's study design, including the interview and PhotoVoice guides and will continued to be consulted throughout the study and its dissemination activities.

title: Energetic metabolism in bipolar disorder: from markers to precision therapeutics.
abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) is marked by recurrent mood episodes and functional impairment. Growing evidence implicates mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and metabolic disturbances as important to its pathophysiology, affecting neuronal signalling, synaptic plasticity, and inflammatory pathways. This review synthesises current evidence linking energetic metabolism to BD, integrates neuroimaging and peripheral biomarker findings, and discusses emerging therapeutic strategies targeting mitochondrial and metabolic dysfunction. A systematic search following PRISMA guidelines was conducted across PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, and Cochrane Library using 'bipolar disorder', 'energetic metabolism', and 'mitochondria'. Inclusion criteria comprised peer-reviewed human studies, original research, and meta-analyses; paediatric, non-English, dietary, genetic, or comorbidity-focused studies were excluded. Additional manual searches targeted biomarker-specific studies. Evidence consistently shows impaired oxidative phosphorylation, reduced ATP and phosphocreatine, altered NAD+/NADH ratios, and increased oxidative and inflammatory markers in BD. Neuroimaging demonstrates reduced PCr/ATP ratios, elevated lactate, and decreased TCA cycle intermediates, indicating cerebral energy deficits. Peripheral biomarkers: including decreased ETC complex activity, increased MDA and 8-OHdG, altered purinergic enzymes, and elevated mtDNA reflect systemic bioenergetic stress. Emerging interventions targeting mitochondrial cofactors (creatine, CoQ10, carnitine, NAC), metabolic strategies (ketogenic diet), and immunomodulatory or purinergic pathway modulators show promise. Emerging evidence suggests that systemic bioenergetic dysregulation may contribute to the pathophysiology of BD. Integrating mitochondrial, metabolic, and inflammatory biomarkers with neuroimaging may enable biologically informed patient stratification and precision therapeutics aimed at restoring energetic homeostasis. Large, standardised multicenter studies are required to translate these findings into clinical practice.

title: GABAergic Network Dysregulation in Alcohol Use Disorder: Receptor-Transporter Interactions Driving the Transition From Goal-Directed to Compulsive Behaviour.
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is characterized by a shift from controlled, goal-directed drinking to compulsive, habitual alcohol (a.k.a. ethanol) seeking, even in the face of negative outcomes. This transition is closely associated with alterations in cortico-striatal circuitry and dysregulated GABAergic signalling, both of which drive the progression from flexible control to compulsive behaviour. Acute alcohol exposure enhances GABAergic inhibition, primarily by increasing presynaptic GABA release. Chronic exposure leads to compensatory neuroadaptations, such as subunit reorganization, receptor internalization and diminished GABA receptor sensitivity. While these neuroadaptations alter receptor-mediated GABAergic signalling during dependence and withdrawal, they also alter dopaminergic regulation and further reinforce alcohol-seeking behaviour. Beyond receptor-level adaptations, impaired GABA clearance, especially through the astrocytic transporter GAT3, plays a crucial role in regulating extracellular GABA concentrations and tonic inhibition. This effect is particularly evident within the dorsal striatum, where elevated tonic GABA shifts control from flexible, goal-directed action towards rigid, habitual responding by altering the balance between the dorsomedial and dorsolateral subregions. Consistent with these mechanistic insights, animal and human studies demonstrate that reduced GAT3 expression is associated with compulsive alcohol use and impaired reward-related behaviour, reinforcing impaired GABA clearance as a central mechanism in this behavioural shift. Taken together, these lines of evidence validate a central therapeutic model, namely, that targeting altered tonic inhibition and impaired GABA clearance in AUD could address the inhibitory dysfunction that sustains the disorder. Overall, this work supports a unifying model in which receptor adaptations and disrupted GABA removal maintain altered inhibitory tone, driving maladaptive circuit function and contributing to the persistence of AUD.

title: Evidence for the Existence of Neural Stem-Like Cells in Adult Rodent Intrinsic Cardiac Nervous Ganglia.
journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology
abstract: Cardiac function is modulated by the intrinsic cardiac nervous system (ICNS), which integrates autonomic signals and undergoes remodeling in pathological conditions. Here, we demonstrate that adult rodent ICNS ganglia harbor neural stem-like cells that proliferate in vitro, form neurospheres, self-renew, and generate neurons expressing βIII-tubulin and PGP 9.5. In vivo, cells expressing the stem cell marker SOX2 are detected within ICNS ganglia. Moreover, cardiac injury induced by monocrotaline increases the number of SOX2-positive cells expressing the cell cycle marker Ki67 and the number of EdU-incorporating, nestin-expressing cells within the ICNS. Together, our data provide the first evidence of neural stem-like cells in adult ICNS ganglia and suggest their potential role in cardiac neuroplasticity.

title: Flipping Patients' Understanding of Pain-Flipped Learning Pain Education Model in Physical Therapy.
abstract: Chronic pain affects more than 1 in 5 adults in the United States. Our understanding of pain has improved, particularly regarding psychosocial factors. Compelling evidence supports pain neuroscience education for chronic pain, but the best methods for implementation in clinical practice remain unclear. The aim was to evaluate the impact of a flipped learning pain education model in physical therapy on the function of patients with chronic pain. In addition, the purpose was to describe the predicted and actual number of physical therapy visits in this population. A retrospective, uncontrolled single-therapist chart review was conducted. Adults diagnosed with chronic pain who received physical therapy using the flipped learning pain education model and had pre- and post-rehabilitation Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS) scores were included. The main outcome was change in the PSFS. The number of predicted visits was derived from the Focus on Therapeutic Outcomes tool. A total of 28 individuals (68% women) were identified. PSFS scores significantly increased from a median of 2.0 (interquartile range, IQR 3.2) to 8.6 (IQR 2.9) (p < 0.001). At baseline, the median predicted number of visits was 12.0 (IQR 4.0), while the median actual visits were 5.0 (IQR 1.8). A total of 24 patients (85.7%) achieved or exceeded the minimal clinically important difference. PSFS scores were higher at the final recorded visit in this selected complete-case cohort receiving physical therapy using a flipped learning model. The findings should be interpreted with caution due to the exploratory nature of the study.

title: Immersive Virtual Reality as a Probe of Context-Dependent Gait Control: Reply to Peh et al.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society

title: Mesenchymal Stem Cell Therapy for Multiple Sclerosis: Harnessing Immunological Properties.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease triggered by damage to the central nervous system (CNS). This CNS damage is caused by the attack of autoreactive T cells against the myelin sheath. Genetic and environmental factors contribute to the development of MS, and the condition causes serious disabilities and exerts substantial health burdens. Although various disease-modifying agents have been developed, they have critical limitations; hence, effective interventions are required. In this context, cell transplantation therapy using mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), hematopoietic stem cells, neural precursors, neural stem cells, and induced pluripotent stem cells is considered a feasible alternative therapeutic approach. MSCs are adult stem cells that differentiate into multiple lineages and exert immunomodulatory, neuroprotective, and neuroregenerative effects. Therefore, MSCs are considered a promising treatment option for MS owing to their ease of isolation and low immunogenicity. This review summarizes the potential therapeutic benefits of the latest MSC-based approaches for MS treatment in animal models and humans. Furthermore, the review discusses the immunological role of MSCs and future directions for their applications.

title: Propofol Modulates Fear Memory Reconsolidation by Inhibiting D2 Receptor-Expressing Neurons in the Medial Prefrontal Cortex.
abstract: Fear memory reconsolidation provides a temporal window for modifying established fear memories, yet the underlying cellular and neural circuit mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Using in vivo fiber photometry and chemogenetic approaches in freely moving mice, we show that propofol modulates fear memory reconsolidation by inhibiting D2 receptor-expressing neurons in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). These neurons exhibit heightened activity during fear memory reconsolidation and project prominently to the basolateral amygdala (BLA). Notably, local pharmacological activation of D2 receptors in the mPFC recapitulates the fear-attenuating effect of propofol when administered during the reconsolidation window. Circuit-level investigations further show that propofol suppresses the reconsolidation-associated enhancement of the mPFCD2-BLA synaptic transmission, and chemogenetic activation of this projection counteracts the effect of propofol on fear memory reconsolidation. Moreover, selective knockdown of D2 receptors in BLA-projecting mPFC neurons diminishes the effect of propofol, supporting a critical role for D2 receptor signaling within this projection-defined circuit. Together, these findings identify the mPFCD2-BLA circuit as a key neural substrate through which propofol modulates fear memory reconsolidation and highlight prefrontal D2 receptor signaling as a potential target for reconsolidation-based interventions aimed at maladaptive fear memories.

title: Establishing Welfare Evacuation Shelters for Children With Medical Complexity: A Prefecture-Wide Policy Shift Driven by Simulation in Tottori, Japan.
journal: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness
abstract: Children with medical complexity (CMC) are highly vulnerable during disasters, yet few Japanese welfare evacuation shelters accept them, leading to hospital-dependent planning. We aimed to assess the key issues hindering the establishment of welfare evacuation shelters for CMC. In Tottori Prefecture (2020-2024), the government, municipalities, a university hospital, and device partners used facility assessments, staff education, and tabletop/field simulations (weekday earthquake with power outage and ventilator-dependent 5-year-old model) to identify gaps and iteratively revise manuals. Key issues included space underestimation, difficult mobility, power insecurity, unreliable verbal information, unclear deterioration pathways, and undefined public health nurse (PHN) roles. Revisions established PHN-led reception/triage, standardized information collection, specified power sourcing, and set escalation/transport flows. A section on "Persons Requiring Medical Care" was added to prefectural policies, and the disaster medical guidance was updated, shifting preparedness from hospital-centered to shelter-based welfare. This simulation-driven intersectoral model appears scalable; however, it was performed in a single prefecture with limited follow-up, impairing generalizability.

title: EEG-based brain effective and functional connectivity predict PET-defined amyloid positivity in cognitively normal individuals.
journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association
abstract: Early identification of amyloid-beta (Aβ) pathology is essential for timely intervention in Alzheimer's disease (AD), as Aβ accumulation precedes clinical symptoms by years. We predicted positron emission tomography (PET) -defined Aβ status in cognitively normal individuals using non-invasive resting-state dry electroencephalography (EEG). Brain effective and functional connectivity were quantified to characterize dynamic information transfer between regions. Features derived from dynamic brain connectivity were used to train machine learning models for Aβ classification. EEG-based models can predict amyloid positivity with accuracy comparable to, or in some cases exceeding, that of plasma p-tau217 and previously reported predictors based on cognitive measures, demographics, and health factors, depending on the model. Beyond near real-time Aβ inference, the framework identifies the most affected brain regions and connections associated with neurodegeneration, offering complementary information to blood-based biomarkers and supporting its potential as an affordable tool for early AD detection in primary care and population screening.

title: EXPRESS: Longitudinal FDG-PET reveals early hypermetabolism associated with astrocyte changes in TgF344-AD rats.
journal: Journal of cerebral blood flow and metabolism : official journal of the International Society of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by alterations in brain glucose metabolism, classically showing [18F]FDG-PET hypometabolism in later stages. However, emerging evidence suggests a transient phase of glucose hypermetabolism early in the disease, for which biological basis remains unclear. We combined longitudinal and cross-sectional approaches in TgF344-AD rats and wild-type controls at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months. Longitudinal assessments included [18F]FDG-microPET imaging, behavioral testing, and cerebrospinal fluid biomarker analysis. Cross-sectional analyses included amyloid histopathology, western blot and ex vivo glutamate uptake measurements. TgF344-AD rats exhibited increased cerebral glucose metabolism at 9mo, predominantly in cortical regions. This phase coincided with emerging cognitive impairment and early amyloid deposition. CSF analyses showed increased GFAP at 9-12mo and reduced S100B at 9mo, while microglial/inflammatory markers remained unchanged. WB confirmed region-specific GFAP alterations without changes in neuronal or synaptic markers. Glutamate uptake was increased in the cortex and hippocampus at 9mo. These findings identify a transient phase of increased glucose metabolism early in disease progression, associated with astrocyte-related changes, suggesting that early hypermetabolism may reflect non-neuronal processes. This has implications for the interpretation of [18F]FDG-PET as a biomarker in early AD and for understanding early physiological responses to AD pathology.

title: A Review of the Roles of Calcium Signaling and Homeostasis in Nicotine Addiction: A Mechanistic Hypothesis Involving ATP2B2/PMCA2 and α7-Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptors.
journal: Medical science monitor : international medical journal of experimental and clinical research
abstract: Calcium (Ca²⁺) signaling is essential for neurotransmitter release, synaptic plasticity, gene expression, and neuronal excitability. Nicotine, the addictive component of tobacco, activates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), including alpha4ß2- and a7-containing receptor subtypes, thereby altering neuronal Ca²⁺ entry. ATP2B2 encodes plasma membrane calcium-transporting ATPase 2 (PMCA2), a neuronal high-affinity Ca²⁺ extrusion pump that helps shape local Ca²⁺ microdomains. Published work has shown that PMCA2 functionally associates with a7-nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (alpha7-nAChRs) through postsynaptic density protein 95 (PSD-95) and can influence a7-nAChR surface expression. Genetic and transcriptomic studies have also linked ATP2B2-related pathways to substance use phenotypes, but there is no direct evidence that chronic nicotine alters PMCA2 expression. This narrative review distinguishes established findings from indirect evidence and untested predictions. We propose a mechanistic hypothesis in which chronic nicotine exposure may establish a new calcium-homeostatic equilibrium characterized by alpha7-nAChR downregulation and compensatory PMCA2 upregulation. We also hypothesize that, during early withdrawal, persistently elevated PMCA2 activity could contribute to excessive Ca²⁺ extrusion, reduced presynaptic glutamate release, cognitive impairment, and relapse vulnerability. These predicted effects require direct testing in nicotine exposure and withdrawal models. This review aims to examine the roles of calcium signaling and homeostasis in nicotine addiction, with particular emphasis on ATP2B2, which encodes the calcium ion pump PMCA2, and alpha7-nAChR.

title: EXPRESS: Targeting the Neurovascular Interface: Endothelial Optogenetics as a New Frontier for Brain Circuit Interrogation.
journal: Journal of cerebral blood flow and metabolism : official journal of the International Society of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism
abstract: The advent of optogenetics has revolutionized neuroscience by enabling precise manipulation of neural circuits, solidifying a neuron-centric view of brain function. This perspective has increasingly expanded to encompass non-neuronal cells, with the optogenetic control of astrocytes, microglia, and pericytes revealing their active roles in information processing. Yet the vascular endothelium long regarded as a passive conduit has remained largely unexplored through this lens. Here we discuss the emerging field of endothelial optogenetics, which seeks to isolate the cell-autonomous signaling capacity of brain endothelial cells, distinct from their hemodynamic functions. We explore the hypothesis that targeted optical stimulation of these cells may evoke calcium-dependent release of angiocrine factors, establishing a vasculature-to-parenchyma signaling axis that directly modulates neuronal activity and behavior. This approach not only challenges the traditional neurovascular coupling paradigm but also offers transformative potential for reinterpreting neuroimaging data and developing novel therapies for neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. By elevating the endothelium to the status of an active computational element, endothelial optogenetics promises to reshape our understanding of the brain as an integrated hemo-neural system.

title: METTL7B-Mediated m6A Modification of PLEKHA4 Suppresses Ferroptosis via Reducing AURKA Ubiquitination to Promote Papillary Thyroid Cancer Progression.
abstract: The malignant progression of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is closely associated with the acquisition of ferroptosis resistance by tumor cells; however, the upstream regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study aims to elucidate the function and molecular mechanisms of the methyltransferase-like 7B (METTL7B)/pleckstrin homology domain-containing family A member 4 (PLEKHA4)/aurora kinase A (AURKA) signaling axis in ferroptosis resistance in PTC. Our results showed that PLEKHA4 was highly expressed in PTC. By binding to kelch-like protein 12 (KLHL12), PLEKHA4 inhibited KLHL12-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of AURKA, thereby stabilizing the AURKA protein and enhancing ferroptosis resistance in PTC cells. Upstream, METTL7B stabilized PLEKHA4 mRNA and upregulated its expression through N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification. Both in vitro and in vivo experiments confirmed that knockdown of METTL7B increased ferroptosis sensitivity and suppressed PTC progression. This study reveals a novel paradigm in which PLEKHA4, as an effector of m6A modification, regulates ferroptosis by interfering with ubiquitin-mediated degradation, providing a theoretical basis for targeting this pathway in the treatment of PTC.

title: The Predictive Value of Infant Ultrasonic Vocalizations in a Longitudinal Study of Maternal Separation in Rats.
abstract: Maternal separation (MS) is a well-established rodent model of early-life stress, implicated in the development of various neuropsychiatric conditions. Infant ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) serve as key communicative signals and have been used to assess early emotional and social development. Here, we examined the long-term behavioral and neurobiological effects of MS across adolescence and adulthood, focusing on the predictive potential of separation-induced infant USVs (40-60 kHz). MS was conducted between postnatal days (PND) 2-14, followed by a maternal potentiation test on PND 15, during which USVs were recorded. Behavioral assessments included anxiety and social play in adolescence (PND 35-36); and anxiety, sociability, anhedonia, and fear memory in adulthood (PND 80-88). MS reduced USVs in the potentiation paradigm, suppressed social play, and ameliorated anxiety-like behavior in adolescence. In adulthood, MS induced anhedonia, impaired fear memory, and decreased c-Fos-immunopositive cells in the lateral amygdala. Path and regression analyses revealed that infant USVs predicted open arm duration in the elevated plus maze in adolescence. USVs were negatively correlated with stress-induced neuronal activation in the habenula in control, but not MS animals. These findings indicate that infant USVs constitute a biobehavioral marker for early-life adverse experiences and predict the development of later affective conditions.

title: Making sense of touch: Spatial tactile cues promote efficient visuo-somatosensory integration and restore motor accuracy under sensory conflict.
abstract: Effective interaction with complex environments relies on the integration of somatosensory and visual signals into coherent spatial representations of the body in external space. When these signals conflict, as during goal-directed hand movements under mirror-reversed visual feedback, motor performance deteriorates. Despite this conflict, the visual mapping between the hand and the environment remains preserved, and visual information typically facilitates motor performance, whereas tactile feedback impairs it. Here, we tested whether providing tactile input with explicit spatial structure renders visuo-somatosensory integration functionally relevant and stabilizes motor behaviour under sensory conflict. Healthy adults performed a mirror-tracing task, tracing a shape's contour with the index finger while tactile feedback conveyed either motion-related cues alone or additional discrete spatial landmarks aligned with the outline. Spatially structured tactile cues preserved movement accuracy and smoothness relative to motion-related tactile input, indicating more effective online motor control. EEG source analyses further revealed that, when spatial tactile cues were present, somatosensory activity increased and functional connectivity was largely restricted to sensorimotor areas. In contrast, when tactile cues did not convey spatial information, sensory conflict was associated with widespread reductions in cortical activity, including in somatosensory and parietal areas, and with a diffuse functional connectivity pattern consistent with elevated sensorimotor uncertainty. Together, these findings indicate that providing spatial structure to tactile input can mitigate the detrimental effects of visuo-somatosensory conflict on motor performance and support more efficient integration of visual and somatosensory information during action. KEY POINTS: Accurate movements depend on combining visual and somatosensory information to estimate the position of the body in external space. When these signals conflict, motor performance usually deteriorates and tactile feedback can become disruptive. We tested whether tactile feedback becomes useful for movement control when it provides explicit spatial landmarks, rather than only motion-related information from finger-surface contact. During a tracing task under visuo-somatosensory conflict, spatially structured tactile cues preserved movement accuracy and smoothness compared with when touch conveyed motion cues alone. Spatial tactile cues were associated with increased somatosensory cortical activity and a more spatially restricted pattern of functional coupling within sensorimotor networks, whereas their absence was associated with reduced somatosensory and parietal activity and a more distributed connectivity profile. Spatial structure in touch promotes multisensory integration, helping stabilize motor control under sensory conflict and highlighting how tactile cue design may improve sensorimotor function.

title: Adverse Pregnancy Outcomes and Early Prediction of Cardiovascular Disease Risk: Vascular and Inflammatory Markers.
abstract: Women with adverse pregnancy outcomes (APOs) have a 2- to 8-fold increased risk of future atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), yet the mechanistic pathways are not well-defined. Potential vascular and inflammatory factors contributing to ASCVD are not known in women with a history of preeclampsia (PE) or spontaneous preterm delivery (sPTD). Describe the vascular and inflammatory factors of women with PE or sPTD and compare differences that may contribute to ASCVD risk. Women 18 years or older, 2-3 years postpartum, with a history of PE (N = 19) or sPTD (N = 13), and reference controls (N = 19; delivery ≥ 37 weeks' gestation without APO) were enrolled. All cohorts underwent phlebotomy to measure inflammatory biomarkers and SphygmoCor testing for vascular function, including augmentation index (AIx75), central pulse pressure (CPP), and pulse wave velocity (PWV). Participants with sPTD had higher interleukin-8 concentrations of 6.6 pg/mL (interquartile range [IQR] 5.7, 8.7), compared with 4.7 pg/mL (IQR 2.2, 6.3) in controls (p = 0.0279). Brachial systolic pressure was higher in PE (120 [standard deviation or SD 12.01]) than in sPTD (110.9 [SD 13.8]) or controls (108.6 [SD 9.22], [p = 0.0071]). Central systolic pressure was higher in PE (109.8 [SD 11.4]) than in sPTD (99.3 [SD 13.88]) or controls (98.4 [SD 8.94], [p = 0.0069]). CPP was higher in PE (34.2, SD 3.62) than in sPTD (30.8, SD 3.34) and controls (30.3, SD 3.67 [p = 0.0027]). Vascular and inflammatory markers in PE or sPTD 2-3 years postpartum are higher compared with reference controls. Future studies should investigate vascular and inflammatory function in larger cohorts and prospectively evaluate contribution to CVD risk.

title: Novel Histamine H3 Receptor Ligands by Integrated Ligand- and Structure-Based Computational Modeling.
abstract: The histamine H3 receptor (H3R) is an attractive central nervous system target due to its regulatory role in histaminergic neurotransmission and its ability to modulate the release of several other neurotransmitters implicated in cognition, arousal, and neurodegenerative disorders. In this study, an integrated chemometric workflow was developed to identify novel H3R ligands by combining structure-based and ligand-based pharmacophore modeling, QSAR analysis, molecular docking, and experimental validation. A structure-based pharmacophore model derived from the H3R crystal structure and a ligand-based pharmacophore model generated from known H3R inhibitors were validated by ROC analysis. The top-performing pharmacophore models showed excellent discrimination between actives and decoys. The QSAR model demonstrated good predictive performance (r2 = 0.75, q2 = 0.78, predicted r2 = 0.67), supporting its application in hit prioritization. The validated pharmacophore models were subsequently used to virtually screen the ChemDiv CNS BBB library of 22 790 compounds. Docking, consensus scoring, and QSAR-guided filtering identified 20 top-ranked hits for experimental evaluation in a [3H]-Nα-methylhistamine displacement assay. One hit, D466-0370 (60), exhibited submicromolar affinity for H3R (Ki = 641 nM), while seven additional compounds showed low micromolar binding affinities. In silico ADMET profiling for the most active hits further supported their compatibility with CNS-relevant chemical space. Overall, this integrated workflow efficiently identified structurally novel H3R ligands with promising biological activities.

title: Artificial Cells and Biomimetic Cells: Intelligent Systems Driving a Paradigm Shift in Drug Discovery and Delivery.
abstract: The convergence of synthetic biology, materials science, and artificial intelligence drives a transformative shift in biopharmaceutical research, advancing from passive drug carriers to intelligent, programmable therapeutics. This review evaluates artificial and biomimetic cells as a framework that connects fundamental biological discovery with clinical translation. It examines five key technological pathways: membrane-engineered artificial cells, membraneless organelle (MLO) systems, multicompartmental artificial cells, protocell communication networks, and virtual cells. These platforms enable precise regulation of drug stability, targeting, biosynthesis, and adaptive responsiveness. Recent progress includes microenvironment-triggered release, logic-gated intercellular communication, and virtual cell-assisted high-throughput screening and toxicity prediction. Despite these advances, challenges remain in scalable manufacturing, long-term stability, and regulatory adaptation. The integration of closed-loop learning, interpretable models, and advanced biomanufacturing will be essential to position artificial and biomimetic cell systems at the forefront of next-generation precision medicine.

title: Radiomic Signatures From Conventional MRI Predict Recovery in Obstetric Brachial Plexus Palsy: A Machine Learning Approach in Infants.
abstract: Obstetric brachial plexus palsy (OBPP) causes variable neurological outcomes, but early prognostic biomarkers remain limited. This study evaluated whether radiomic features extracted from routine T2-STIR MRI can predict functional recovery in infants with OBPP, and whether combining these features with routinely available clinical predictors improves prognostic performance. In this prospective single-center study, 39 infants with OBPP (mean age 12.5 ± 5.7 weeks) underwent 3 T MRI during physiological sleep. Postganglionic lesions were semi-automatically segmented on coronal T2-STIR images, and 111 radiomic features were extracted per patient. After a minimum two-year clinical follow-up (mean 25.5 ± 2.0 months; range 24-32 months), patients were classified as having complete (n = 17) or partial recovery (n = 22). Feature selection was performed using the Boruta algorithm. Five supervised machine learning models were trained and internally optimized on the training set (n = 28) using leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV), and their performance was subsequently evaluated on an independent holdout test set (n = 11). A clinical model (Narakas classification, birth weight, pseudomeningocele) and a combined clinical-radiomic model, summarized as a nomogram, were additionally developed. Eight radiomic features, including shape, first-order, and texture metrics, differentiated recovery groups. Among the radiomics-only models, SVM-RBF performed best (training AUC = 0.929, F1-score = 0.889; test AUC = 0.867, F1-score = 0.750), followed by random forest (training AUC = 0.952; test AUC = 0.783); test-set specificity was low for several classifiers. The combined clinical-radiomic model outperformed the radiomics-only model (training AUC = 1.000; test AUC = 0.933, accuracy = 0.818), and the bias-corrected calibration curve of the nomogram showed good agreement with observed outcomes (mean absolute error = 0.07). Radiomic analysis of routine T2-STIR MRI shows promise for predicting recovery in OBPP, and its combination with simple clinical predictors further improves discrimination. Given the small sample size and the performance drop between training and test sets, these findings should be regarded as preliminary and hypothesis-generating, and require validation in larger, multicenter cohorts before clinical use.

title: Serotonin signaling enhances phagocytosis by brain macrophages through Htr2b and alleviates brain injury after stroke.
abstract: Brain myeloid cells, including infiltrating monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) and microglia, play critical roles in ischemic brain injury, clearing debris and shaping neuroinflammation and neurological outcomes. Yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, using single-cell RNA sequencing and fate mapping with an MDM-specific Ms4a3creERT2-Ai14 mouse line, we identified serotonin receptor Htr2b+ MDMs as a crucial cell population involved in resolving neuroinflammation within the ischemic penumbra. Htr2b+ MDMs significantly accumulate in the peri-infarct region and exhibit enhanced phagocytosis and inflammation-resolving gene signatures. Mechanistically, Htr2b activation promotes nuclear translocation of Tfe3, a key lysosomal regulator, enhancing lysosomal biogenesis and supporting phagocytic activity. MDM-specific Htr2b ablation impairs debris clearance, exacerbates neuroinflammation and ischemic injury, whereas pharmacological agonism or Tfe3 activation restores lysosomal biogenesis in brain MDMs and improves post-stroke outcomes. Thus we demonstrate a previously unrecognized Htr2b+ MDM subset that integrates serotonin signaling to license intrinsic phagocytic function, alleviating ischemic brain injury.

title: The brain liquidates billions of mutant neurons around the time we're born.
Meta-study sparks questions about what it means to be good at regulating emotions.
Alzheimer's disease genetics converges on microglial and neuronal dysregulation.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia, with global case numbers projected to reach 153 million in 20501. AD is highly heritable, with twin-based heritability estimates of 60-80%2. Although 1,200 causal loci are predicted to exist for AD3, approximately 80 loci have been associated with AD in two recent studies4,5. Low single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based heritability estimates have prompted the suggestion that little further common-variant risk remains to be found6. Here we analysed data from 109,479 cases, 74,141 proxy cases, 2,131,799 controls and 499,708 proxy controls from diverse ancestries, identifying 118 loci in a multi-ancestry analysis and 9 additional loci in ancestry-specific analyses, 48 of which are new. We identified new AD risk genes, prioritized potential drug targets, and found that genes upregulated in microglia and downregulated in neurons in cases compared with controls were enriched for AD-associated genetic risk. Moreover, we improved polygenic prediction and estimated a SNP heritability of 16%, nearly threefold higher than previous estimates. Together, our findings show that the common-variant contribution to AD has been substantially underestimated, and reveal new molecular and cellular mechanisms as well as specific targets for future drug development research.

title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking.
abstract: Animal locomotion relies on rhythmic body movements driven by central pattern generators (CPGs): neural circuits that produce oscillating output without oscillating input. However, the circuit structure of a CPG for walking is not known in any animal1,2. To identify the cells and synapses that underlie rhythmic leg movement in walking flies, we developed dynamic simulations of the Drosophila ventral nerve cord connectomes3-6. A computational activation screen of descending neurons from the central brain identified DNg100-a known command neuron for walking-as the strongest driver of rhythmic leg motor activity. Simulated network pruning isolated a minimal rhythm-generating circuit consisting of one inhibitory and two excitatory interneurons; this three-neuron circuit was necessary and sufficient for motor rhythms across all six legs and in four connectome datasets. Simulations also predicted that a separate descending pathway (DNb08) drives rhythmic leg movements, which we confirmed experimentally using optogenetics in behaving flies. Our results reveal the cellular identity and synaptic structure of a putative CPG circuit for walking and other rhythmic leg movements in flies.

title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature.
abstract: Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits2, prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person's capacity to regulate emotions3-5. Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity-trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation-do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons.
abstract: Human neurons are postmitotic and long-lived, requiring precise genomic regulation. Normal neuronal function is highly dosage-sensitive, with copy number variants (CNVs) and heterozygous point mutations associated with a host of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions1-4. Here we investigated somatic CNVs arising in single neurons to understand the dynamic processes that shape the normal neuronal genetic landscape. Altogether, we sequenced 2,357 single neurons from human postmortem brain from fetal to postnatal life. Two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches-Tn5-transposase-based amplification (1,526 neurons, 16 individuals) and primary template amplification5 (831 neurons, 12 individuals)-showed that an average of 25.9% [12.7-46%] of prenatal cortical neurons have highly aberrant genomes, that is, widespread CNVs involving multiple chromosomes. This proportion reduced by about 4.5-fold after birth across the two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches (Fisher meta-analysis P = 3.5 × 10-6). Neurons with widespread CNVs were mainly eliminated perinatally, timed roughly parallel to periods of programmed cell death6, whereas neurons with smaller CNV burdens declined slowly in frequency with postnatal age. CNVs in surviving neurons were depleted for dosage-sensitive genes and genes involved in neurodevelopmental disorders (hypergeometric test P < 0.05), suggesting selective elimination of neurons with these CNVs. Analysis of 44,861 nuclei with single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (snATAC) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) showed that neurons with high CNV burdens exhibited abnormal synaptic gene expression, suggesting that abnormal synaptic gene regulation contributes to neuronal elimination. Elimination of defective neuronal genomes might represent an important developmental genome quality-control process that may be vulnerable in neurodevelopmental disease, and suggests purifying selection during human neurodevelopment.

title: Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers.
abstract: The N7-methylguanosine (m7G) modification is one of the most prevalent tRNA modifications, mainly catalysed by the METTL1-WDR4 protein complex1-4. The m7G methyltransferase METTL1 has been linked to oncogenic transformation and the maintenance of several aggressive malignancies; however, the clinical implications of therapeutically targeting a tRNA-modifying enzyme have not been established. Here we present the development and characterization of STM9005, a highly selective and potent first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor of METTL1. Treatment of numerous cancer cell models (including leukaemia, melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma, oesophageal cancer and small cell lung carcinoma) with STM9005 blocks cell growth, causes differentiation changes and dysregulates cell cycle progression. These cellular effects were accompanied by a selective decrease in m7G on a subset of tRNAs and a reduction in their expression levels, which impacted the translation of oncogenic mRNAs. We show that pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 in vivo impairs tumour growth and significantly prolongs survival in multiple mouse cancer models of different tissue origin. Collectively, our results provide a strong proof of concept that targeting of tRNA methylation is a promising avenue of anti-cancer therapy and illustrate that catalytic inhibition of METTL1 represents a therapeutic strategy against a number of aggressive malignancies.

title: Presynaptic homeostasis mediated by exocytosis of a SNARE protein.
abstract: The neural plasticity that underlies adaptation and learning requires countervailing homeostatic mechanisms to maintain the stability and responsiveness of neural circuits. Previous work has described several forms of synaptic homeostasis1, but the mechanisms that detect changes in activity and transduce these into altered neurotransmission have remained poorly understood. Here we show that high-frequency stimulation alters the subsequent properties of neurotransmitter release to confer a presynaptic form of homeostasis, independent of postsynaptic receptors. The mechanism involves vesicular SNARE protein (v-SNARE) VAMP7 (vesicle-associated membrane protein 7), which reduces neurotransmitter release by inhibiting the entry of Ca2+ specifically through P/Q-type presynaptic Ca2+ channels. Previous work has implicated target SNARE proteins (t-SNAREs) in the inhibition of Ca2+ channels2, but without clear physiological rationale. We show that the activity-dependent regulation of release mediated by VAMP7 requires the t-SNARE syntaxin. Although VAMP7 acts at the plasma membrane to inhibit P/Q-type channels, it localizes predominantly to a subset of synaptic vesicles made by adaptor protein-3 (AP-3) that respond specifically to high-frequency stimulation3,4. The localization of VAMP7 to AP-3-derived synaptic vesicles thus provides a mechanism for the activity-dependent delivery of VAMP7 to the plasma membrane, where it associates with syntaxin to inhibit P/Q-type Ca2+ channels and transmitter release. This homeostatic form of metaplasticity operates at multiple excitatory synapses, and in its absence, the fraction of FOS+ neurons increases several fold, revealing a general property of excitatory neurotransmission that might also maintain the sparsity of neural connections.

title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury.
abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3-5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood-brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood-brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin-CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

title: The grand plan to transform psychiatry - by personalizing mental-health care.
An engineered, compact Cas12m variant for multiplexed gene activation in vivo.
abstract: Achieving coordinated CRISPR-based transactivation (CRISPRa) regulation in vivo remains challenging, as the requisite genetic elements frequently exceed the packaging capacity of AAV vectors. Here we report the identification and engineering of the Cas12m protein family, a naturally nuclease-dead CRISPR system that possesses intrinsic self-processing activity for its precursor crRNA. We develop an optimized variant, denCas12m, and leverage it in the smCRISPRa platform. We show that a single transcriptional unit encoding a multi-gRNA array can be processed into individual functional guides within a target cell, enabling efficient synergistic activation of a single gene through multiple sites or simultaneous activation of distinct endogenous genes from a single all-in-one AAV vector. We demonstrate phenotypic rescue in mouse models of Duchenne muscular dystrophy and Scn1a haploinsufficiency. Furthermore, a single all-in-one AAV vector supports the simultaneous activation of multiple distinct endogenous genes in mice, with a single vector delivering up to eight crRNAs for activation of six different genes, demonstrating the platform's high-order multiplexing.

title: Involuntary Treatment in First-Episode Psychosis and Mania: A Retrospective Population-Based Cohort Study.
abstract: The study aimed to examine how involuntary status at first presentation affects 5-year trajectories of first-episode psychosis or first-episode mania (FEP/FEM). The authors conducted a population-based cohort study on FEP/FEM. Legal status at first episode was classified as involuntary or voluntary. Participants were followed up to 5 years to examine relapse, emergency department use, vocational status, and Social and Occupational Functioning Assessment Scale (SOFAS) scores. Relapse was compared by using log-rank tests; repeated-measures outcomes used mixed-effects models that adjusted for age and sex, with linear, logistic, or negative binomial regression as appropriate. The cohort included 200 individuals (voluntary, N=139; involuntary, N=61). The involuntary group was older than the voluntary group (p<0.001) and had greater illness severity (Clinical Global Impressions-Severity mean=5.5 vs. 5.1, p=0.002) at FEP/FEM. Time to relapse did not differ, nor did emergency department visits or psychiatric hospitalizations. Functioning improved at a similar rate in both groups; however, the involuntary group remained lower in functioning (SOFAS mean difference=-5.9, p=0.007) and had higher odds of being vocationally disengaged throughout follow-up (odds ratio=3.82, p=0.009). The authors found that involuntary treatment at FEP/FEM is common and is characterized by greater baseline illness severity. Involuntary status can serve as an entry point into care without excess long-term service utilization, and both groups showed similar rates of functional improvement. Persistently lower functioning and higher odds of vocational disengagement in the involuntary group support the need for targeted vocational interventions.

title: ADP-ribose induces neuronal ferroptosis through ENT2-mediated nucleotide rewiring.
abstract: Excessive nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) consumption fuels neurological pathogenesis, yet the limited benefit of NAD+ supplementation hints at unresolved toxicity from its catabolism. Here, we identify ADP-ribose, a neglected NAD+ catabolite generated by poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) and poly(ADP-ribose) glycohydrolase, as an inducer of neuronal ferroptosis through nucleotide metabolic rewiring. We discovered that extracellular ADP-ribose directly binds and inhibits the nucleoside transporter equilibrative nucleoside transporter 2 (ENT2; SLC29A2), suppressing nucleotide salvage and driving compensatory hyperactivation of de novo purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis. This metabolic rerouting engages xanthine oxidase (XO) and dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) to unleash superoxide bursts, triggering lipid peroxidation and ferroptotic neuronal death. ADP-ribose accumulates across neurological disease models and its acute administration recapitulates ferroptotic neurodegeneration in vivo. Targeting ADP-ribose signaling through PARP1 knockdown, NUDT9-mediated hydrolysis or dual XO/DHODH inhibition rescues delayed cognitive deficits in intracerebral hemorrhage models. These findings define the ADP-ribose-ENT2 axis as a metabolic driver of neuronal ferroptosis and reveal a druggable vulnerability in disorders marked by NAD+ hyperconsumption.

title: Synaptic transmission and plasticity: molecular mechanisms, biological functions and therapeutic opportunities in neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract: Synaptic transmission impairment and neuronal loss are hallmarks of neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs). To date, the absence of effective therapies for treating or preventing NDDs underscores the critical need to comprehend the mechanisms underlying synaptic loss and impairment to develop novel interventions. Synaptic transmission is a complex communication process between presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons. Separate postsynaptic receptors activated by a variety of neurotransmitters initiate different downstream signaling cascades that are modulated by receptor-associated auxiliary subunits. Moreover, glia-neuron interactions and various neuropeptides can also modulate diverse synaptic functions. In this review, we first summarize the presynaptic and postsynaptic regulatory mechanisms of synaptic transmission in glutamatergic, GABAergic, cholinergic, and dopaminergic neurons in NDDs. We then emphasize the fundamental role of microglia and astrocytes in maintaining neuronal homeostasis and discuss how glia-neuron cross-talk affects synaptic and neuronal function throughout the pathological processes of NDDs, as well as how aging accelerates synaptic dysfunction in NDDs. We also highlight therapeutic strategies aimed at preserving or restoring synaptic integrity, including approaches that enhance plasticity, fine‑tune neurotransmitter signaling, or target immune pathways. Finally, we evaluate the current state of research for each intervention class and consider the major obstacles and opportunities that lie ahead in developing effective synapse‑directed therapies for NDDs.

title: Hippocampal Subfield Volumes and Spatial Memory Performance in Older Adults At-Risk for Type 2 Diabetes.
abstract: Older adults at risk for type 2 diabetes (T2D) are more likely to experience accelerated cognitive aging and neurodegeneration due to impaired metabolism in the hippocampus. However, the precise relationship between T2D risk factors, brain volumes (i.e., gray matter, white matter, hippocampus subfields), and hippocampus-dependent functions (i.e., spatial pattern separation, a component of spatial memory) remains unexplored. To investigate these relationships in this cross-sectional study, 60 older adults at risk for T2D (e.g., high BMI or elevated A1c levels) completed a touchscreen-based spatial pattern separation behavioral task-the Trial-Unique delayed Nonmatching-to-Location (TUNL) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). HippUnfold was utilized to segment the hippocampus from high-resolution, T1-weighted images. We found positive correlations between A1c levels and volumes of the dentate gyrus (DG) and cornu ammonis (CA) 2, indicating that higher A1c was associated with larger volumes of hippocampal subregions. Additionally, TUNL accuracy was correlated with gray matter and distinct hippocampus subfield volumes (i.e., subiculum, CA1, and CA4), with larger volumes associated with better spatial memory performance. Understanding early structural changes in T2D risk allows us to further characterize changes in brain health associated with metabolic dysfunction.

title: There is a biological substrate to being a dad; we should tap into it.

Corrigendum to "Attenuation of postoperative cognitive dysfunction by Mongolian medical warm acupuncture associates with suppressed neuroinflammation and preserved synaptic structural plasticity" [Exp. Neurol. 403 (2026) 115841].
Bacteroidota-derived glycine lipids differentially regulate skeletal muscle mitochondrial adaptation during Western diet feeding in male Ldlr-/- mice.
abstract: The Western diet (WD) is associated with skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired oxidative metabolism, redox imbalance and inflammation. Emerging evidence suggests that gut microbiome-derived metabolites contribute to host metabolic regulation, yet the role of Bacteroidota-derived glycine lipids in skeletal muscle remains unknown. This study tested whether two structurally related bacterial glycine lipids, lipid 654 (L654) and lipid 1256 (L1256), regulate skeletal muscle mitochondrial remodelling in WD-fed Ldlr-/- mice. Male Ldlr-/- mice were fed a normal chow or WD and administered L654, L1256 or vehicle control for 8 weeks. Skeletal muscle glycine lipid accumulation, mitochondrial respiration, mitochondrial biogenesis markers, mitophagy-associated signalling, inflammatory and antioxidant proteins and muscle fibre cross-sectional area were assessed. L1256, but not L654, accumulated in skeletal muscle. Functionally, L1256 selectively enhanced fatty acid-supported mitochondrial respiration and increased respiratory control ratio. L1256 also increased peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and electron transport chain complexes IV and V, suggesting enhanced oxidative mitochondrial remodelling. In parallel, L1256 altered markers associated with mitochondrial quality control signalling, increased nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), suppressed nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) signalling and preserved muscle fibre cross-sectional area. L654 upregulated mitochondrial biogenesis transcripts without altering protein abundance. These findings identify L1256 as a microbiome-derived lipid retained within skeletal muscle that enhanced oxidative metabolism and preserved mitochondrial quality signalling under metabolic stress. The data suggest that tissue retention of bacterial lipids may be an important determinant of skeletal muscle mitochondrial adaptation. KEY POINTS: Western diet contributes to skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired oxidative metabolism and chronic inflammation. Microbiome-derived glycine lipids are bioactive molecules from Bacteroidota species, but their effects on skeletal muscle mitochondrial metabolism remain poorly understood. Bacteroidota-derived glycine lipids produce distinct skeletal muscle responses in Western diet-fed Ldlr- / - mice, where lipid 1256 accumulated in skeletal muscle and enhanced fatty acid-supported respiration, whereas lipid 654 primarily induced transcriptional responses without detectable tissue accumulation. Lipid 1256 increased peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and complexes IV and V of the electron transport chain together with restoration of Parkin, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) while reducing nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) and interleukin 6 (IL-6) expression and preserving skeletal muscle cross-sectional area. These findings suggest that gut microbiome-derived glycine lipids are regulators of skeletal muscle mitochondrial metabolism, and that tissue retention of bacterial lipids influences mitochondrial oxidative remodelling during metabolic stress.

title: Clozapine Augmentation Strategies and Clinical Predictors of Prolonged Tertiary Hospitalization in Clozapine-Resistant Schizophrenia: a Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Clozapine-resistant schizophrenia (CRS) remains a major clinical challenge, with persistent symptoms and functional impairment despite adequate clozapine treatment. Real-world evidence is limited, and guidelines recommend a narrow set of augmentation strategies-aripiprazole (D2/3R partial agonist), amisulpride (D2/3R selective antagonist), and electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)-without clear guidance on selection or sequencing. This study examined augmentation choice and its association with length of stay (LOS) and symptomatic outcomes. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using BC Psychosis Program electronic records (2012-2025). Symptom severity and functioning scores (PANSS, CGI-S, GAPS, SOFAS) were extracted at admission and discharge. Multivariable Cox models assessed LOS for index and discharge augmentation strategies. ANCOVA compared symptom change across discharge strategies. A machine-learning model examined predictors of ECT versus pharmacological augmentation at discharge. Eighty-eight admissions were included. In adjusted index models, D2/3R selective antagonism was associated with shorter LOS than ECT (HR 2.50, 95% CI 1.35-4.62); partial agonism was not (HR 1.41, 95% CI 0.75-2.63). Partial agonist augmentation had the highest inefficacy-related switching. By discharge strategy, ECT was associated with greater reduction in positive symptoms than selective antagonism (MD -3.20, 95% CI -5.65 to -0.75) and partial agonism (MD -3.87, 95% CI -6.57 to -1.16). Greater impairment in psychosis and functioning on admission predicted ECT at discharge (AUC 0.74; balanced accuracy 0.72). D2/3R selective antagonism was the most resource-efficient strategy, while ECT produced greater improvement in positive symptoms. Incorporating baseline psychosis severity and functioning into measurement-based care may support more informed augmentation selection.

title: Content Validity and Psychometric Properties Assessment of the Virtual Reality Functional Capacity Assessment Tool and Application in Multiregional Clinical Trials of Cognitive Impairment Associated with Schizophrenia.
abstract: Cognitive impairment associated with schizophrenia (CIAS) substantially impacts daily living and is a valuable prognostic indicator of functional outcomes in people living with schizophrenia. The Virtual Reality Functional Capacity Assessment Tool (VRFCAT) is used to assess functional capacity, facilitating the development of new treatments for cognitive impairment. This paper aims to provide evidence supporting the use of the VRFCAT as a valid and reliable performance outcome measure to assess functional change (ie, a fit-for-purpose clinical outcome assessment instrument). This paper is divided into two parts. In Part 1, published and unpublished evidence regarding the suitability of the VRFCAT is synthesized, focusing on content validity, including concept mapping to an updated CIAS conceptual model informed by patient input and evaluation, and known psychometric properties. In Part 2, data collected from three multinational CIAS clinical trials are used to evaluate additional psychometric properties (practice effects, test-retest, and convergent validity) and assess the utility of the VRFCAT within its intended context of use. Published literature supports content validity and key psychometric properties of the VRFCAT. The VRFCAT demonstrates alignment with the signs, symptoms, and impacts in the CIAS conceptual model. Analysis of clinical trial data substantiates published psychometric properties within the intended context of use, with no practice effects identified. These findings provide evidence that the VRFCAT is a valid and reliable performance outcome measure for use in assessing functional capacity in people with CIAS, supporting its suitability for use in clinical trials.

title: Neurometabolic Differences in Psychosis Observed with 7 T Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy.
abstract: Altered brain chemistry is thought to contribute to impaired cognition and perceptual functioning in people with psychotic psychopathology (PwPP). As heritable genetic factors shape the development of psychosis, alterations in brain chemistry may extend to biological relatives of PwPP. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) is a non-invasive method for quantifying concentrations of various neurochemicals in the human brain. Previous studies using MRS have generally focused on specific diagnoses (eg, schizophrenia), rather than PwPP trans-diagnostically, and comparably few studies have examined relatives. The goal of the current study was to assess neurometabolic differences in PwPP and relatives using MRS in a large number of participants. As part of the Psychosis Human Connectome Project, we acquired ultra-short echo time (8 ms) MRS data at 7 tesla in both occipital and prefrontal cortices from 64 PwPP, 42 first-degree biological relatives, and 43 controls. We observed lower levels of N-acetyl-aspartate (NAA) in the occipital lobe in PwPP and relatives versus controls, and a trend toward lower N-acetyl-aspartylglutamate in prefrontal cortex in PwPP versus controls. Lower OCC NAA levels were also evident in diagnostic subgroups of PwPP (schizophrenia and bipolar disorder) compared to controls. We also observed higher levels of glucose in both occipital and prefrontal cortices in PwPP. Hierarchical clustering analyses showed that higher glucose levels were linked to higher psychiatric symptoms, poorer cognition, and impaired visual task performance. Together, our findings point to alterations in neural metabolism across multiple brain areas in PwPP that are associated with impaired cognitive and perceptual functioning.
